title: Hypergraph Turán / Erdős–Ko–Rado: the family of 'divisor sets in class' as an intersecting family
connection: Fix p. For each C, S_C = divisors of 4Cp+1 in class −1 mod 4C. The family {S_C} over C — are the sets pairwise 'related' (e.g. a divisor a of 4Cp+1 and a' of 4C'p+1 have gcd structure: gcd(4Cp+1, 4C'p+1) | (C − C')·4p... so gcd divides 4(C' − C))? That bounds how much two S_C can overlap — an 'almost disjointness' that makes the counting cleaner.
why: Near-disjointness of the certificate sets across C means the total count Σ|S_C| has small variance from overlaps — relevant to the second-moment approach and to 'at least one is nonempty' bookkeeping.
first_step: Prove gcd(4Cp+1, 4C'p+1) | 4(C−C')·… precisely; then the divisors in S_C ∩ S_{C'} are ≤ 4|C − C'| — tiny. Record the lemma.

title: Matroids / linear algebra over F₂: the 'sign vectors' of divisors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^×/squares
connection: (ℤ/4C)^× modulo squares is an F₂-vector space; prime factors of 4Cp+1 give vectors; −1 is a target vector; subset-product hits −1 in the quotient iff −1 ∈ span (a linear algebra question!). The full condition (−1 as a subset product, not mod squares) is harder, but the F₂-relaxation is linear and decidable by rank.
why: The F₂-relaxation is a necessary condition for a win that is *linear* — and its failure probability is exactly 2^{−(rank deficiency)}; it isolates the 'genus-like' part (characters of order 2) from the rest. Repo's 'genus layer is pointwise free' lemma may be this.
first_step: git grep -il 'genus layer' -- '*.md' and compare; then compute for p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 100: does the F₂-relaxation hold (−1 ∈ span of factor vectors mod squares) and how often does the full condition fail when the relaxation holds?

title: Gate G4 quantified: 'subgroup generated by factors contains −1' vs 'subset product hits −1' disagree in ~20% of (p, C) pairs
connection: Sanity computation: for primes p < 3000 (p ≡ 1 mod 4) and C < 40, the subgroup generated by the prime factors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^× contains −1 but no subset product (with multiplicities) equals −1 in 1695 of 8229 cases (~21%). So the 'Galois/subgroup' relaxation is far from tight: multiplicity (few factors) matters a lot.
why: Quantifies the repo's gate G4 ('class, not parity'): any proof via 'some prime factor lands outside a subgroup' loses ~20% of the certificates per C, which matters when the expected count per C is < 1.
first_step: Break down the 21% by ω(4Cp+1) (expect: mostly ω ≤ 2); check whether for ω ≥ 4 the two notions agree ≥ 95%; if so, 'C with 4Cp+1 having ≥ 4 prime factors' is a regime where the Galois relaxation is essentially exact.

title: C = 2 parity escape: if 8p+1 = x² − 2y² then C=2 certificate ⟺ some prime factor ≡ 7 mod 8 — and the number of such factors has a parity formula via the norm from ℚ(√2)
connection: 8p + 1 = N(x + y√2) = x² − 2y²: all prime factors are ≡ ±1 mod 8 (or 2, excluded as 8p+1 odd). The C=2 C-form certificate needs a divisor ≡ 7 mod 8 ⟺ at least one prime factor ≡ 7 mod 8 (since the ≡ 1 ones can't help; and any single ≡ 7 factor is a certificate). Number of ≡ 7 factors (with multiplicity) is even (product ≡ 1 mod 8). So C = 2 wins ⟺ 8p+1 is a norm from ℤ[√2] with NOT all factors ≡ 1 mod 8. Is 8p+1 always a norm from ℤ[√2]? No — need (2/q) = 1 for all q ∥ 8p+1 to odd power... So the C=2 analysis splits: either 8p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3,5 mod 8 — then that factor is not ≡ −1 mod 8 and doesn't directly certify, but a product of a ≡ 3 and a ≡ 5 factor is ≡ 15 ≡ 7 ✓ certifies! So C = 2 wins iff the prime factors of 8p+1 (mod 8) admit a subset product ≡ 7 — i.e. NOT(all factors ≡ 1) AND NOT(all non-1 factors are in a single class {3} or {5} with... ) — exactly the subset-product condition. Enumerate the failure patterns mod 8.
why: For C ≤ 3 the failure conditions are fully explicit finite patterns on the multiset of prime residues; listing them exactly is the base case for the 'failure taxonomy' and for a potential 'C ≤ K failure ⟹ contradiction' argument.
first_step: For C = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6: list the exact failure patterns on multisets of prime residues mod 4C; compute densities; verify against data.

title: Ask: is there any (p, C) failure with ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 6 where D is NOT a union of cosets of a nontrivial subgroup? (Kneser-periodicity test of 'rich' failures)
connection: If rich failures (many prime factors) are always periodic (D = union of H-cosets with H ∌ −1 and H nontrivial), then failures split cleanly into 'poor' (ω ≤ 5) and 'periodic'. The periodic ones are controlled by Galois (all factors in a subgroup); the poor ones by sieve (few prime factors is rare across C). A proof could treat the two regimes separately. [Partial answer from a quick check with Ω ≥ 5: yes, the majority (61%) of rich failures are NOT subgroup-type; the stabiliser computation remains to be done.]
why: Sharp empirical dichotomy test with direct proof-strategy consequences.
first_step: Scan p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 200 for failures with ω ≥ 6; compute stabilisers.

title: Finding: 'rich' C-form failures are mostly multiplicity-poverty, not subgroup obstructions (61% vs 39%)
connection: For p < 6000, C < 150: of 4182 failing (p, C) with Ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 5, the prime factors generate a subgroup containing −1 in 2531 cases (61%) — the failure is that no subset product with the available multiplicities equals −1 — and generate a −1-free subgroup in 1651 cases (39%). So even with ≥ 5 prime factors the subset-product set D (|D| ≤ 2^Ω ≤ 32 vs φ(4C) up to ~300) is simply too small to be forced to contain −1.
why: Kills the clean 'rich ⟹ Galois-type failure' dichotomy that would have made a sieve-over-norm-conditions proof sketch viable; shows the binding constraint is |D| ≪ φ(4C) (Davenport-constant regime), i.e. the probabilistic regime starts at very small C. Any pointwise argument must live in the regime C ≤ (log p)^{log 2} where 2^Ω can exceed φ(4C), or must be genuinely probabilistic.
first_step: Redo with distinct-prime count ω and with the threshold |D| ≥ φ(4C): find the fraction of (p, C) where D could in principle cover the group; check whether in THAT regime failures are always subgroup-type (which would restore a dichotomy in the only regime where it matters).

title: Sylvester's sequence and the extremal 1 = Σ1/x_i problem as a dual
connection: Sylvester's sequence gives extremal denominators in Σ1/x_i = 1 ↔ ES's largest denominator is bounded by p²·(…); extremal structure constrains solution shape.
why: Bounding the largest denominator in any ES solution (Curtiss/Soundararajan-type bounds) restricts the search space and may give a finite-check argument shape.
first_step: Compute max(z)/p² over all ES solutions for primes ≤ 10⁵ and compare to Curtiss-type extremal bounds.

title: Sidon/B_h sets: are ES solution denominators 'too structured' to avoid?
connection: Sets avoiding solutions to 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n-type linear-in-reciprocals equations ↔ Ruzsa's theory of sets without solutions of linear equations.
why: Ruzsa-type extremal results for reciprocal equations might give: the set of 'certificate parameters' is too large to avoid the ES hyperplane.
first_step: Search literature: 'sets without solutions to 1/x + 1/y = 1/z' density (Erdős problem) — record what's known.

title: Percolation on the divisor graph: does p 'percolate' to a certificate?
connection: Divisor-lattice percolation ↔ ES certificate as a connection path in a graph whose nodes are p-tied integers and edges are divisibility in classes.
why: Percolation has sharp threshold theorems (Friedgut–Kalai); a giant-component argument could give existence when density exceeds a threshold.
first_step: Define graph G_p on {4Cp+1 : C ≤ T} ∪ divisors with edges by residue condition; compute component sizes for hard vs easy p.

title: Bohr sets / Bohr neighbourhoods of p: certificates as elements of a Bohr set
connection: Bohr set B(Γ,ε) = {x : ‖γx‖ < ε} ↔ ES certificates require p/m near −u/m exactly (ε = 0).
why: Additive-combinatorics machinery on Bohr sets gives structure for 'approximate' ES; exact would need ε < 1/m.
first_step: Compute, per p, the approximate certificate count with tolerance ε = k/m for k ≤ K and check if exact count ≈ approximate/(2K+1).

title: Benjamini–Schramm / local limit of the 'divisor graph' around p
connection: Local weak limits of graphs ↔ the neighbourhood structure of p in the ES certificate graph.
why: Too abstract unless a concrete graph emerges; keep as curiosity.
first_step: Define graph: vertices = primes ≤ X, edge p~q if they share a certificate modulus; compute degree distribution.

title: Cryptographic hardness assumption: 'ES-certificate search is hard' as a one-way function candidate
connection: If certificates were hard to find but easy to verify, p ↦ certificate is a NP-search; crypto reductions require average-case hardness ↔ ES almost-all results suggest easy on average.
why: Fun meta: certificate search is easy heuristically (small C works), so ES gives no OWF; that easiness itself is evidence of a uniform algorithm.
first_step: Quantify: over primes ≤ 10⁹, distribution of the work (number of trials) to find the first certificate; if max work is polylog, conjecture a 'polylog search time' strengthening.

title: Supersaturation: ES certificates as copies of a small 'pattern' in a dense p-dependent structure
connection: Supersaturation (Erdős–Simonovits, Blakley–Roy) yields many copies of a pattern in any dense enough host ↔ define a host structure H_p (e.g. a bipartite graph between u and C with edges for (4uC−1) | p+u...?) — edges are the certificates themselves, so need a pattern built from easier objects.
why: If certificates could be expressed as copies of a pattern in a host whose density is forced (e.g. by divisor counts of an interval), Blakley–Roy-type inequalities give pointwise counts.
first_step: Look for a host graph G_p with ≫ p edges (e.g. pairs (a,b) with ab ≡ 1 mod something tied to p) where a 4-cycle or path of length 2 corresponds to an ES certificate; then apply Sidorenko-type lower bounds.

title: Sidorenko / Blakley–Roy: homomorphism counts of paths in a 'divisibility graph'
connection: Blakley–Roy: hom(P_k, G) ≥ n·d^k in any graph — pointwise lower bound from density ↔ ES certificate as a path of length 2 in a graph whose average degree is computable at p.
why: Gives a pointwise count lower bound purely from the edge count — a rare pointwise mechanism. The difficulty: certificates must be exactly the paths (all paths), which needs a clever graph.
first_step: Try G_p on vertex set ℤ/M with edges a~b iff ab ≡ (something with p) mod M; check whether 2-paths correspond to Type II certificates for some modulus choice; test on p ≤ 100.

title: Matroid / independence structure of divisor classes mod 4C
connection: Classes of prime factors as vectors in (ℤ/4C)^× ⊗ F_2 ↔ matroid rank decides 2-part of gate.
why: Ties to F₂-linear-algebra item; matroid union theorems might handle multiple C simultaneously.
first_step: For each C compute matroid of 2-adic character vectors of prime factors of 4Cp+1; study rank deficiency for hard p.

title: Egyptian-fraction 'tree of all solutions' as a graph: connected via common denominators
connection: Graph whose nodes are solutions for all n ≤ X, edges when they share two denominators ↔ moves between solutions of different n.
why: If moves are local (n changes by small structured amounts), the graph could support induction-like arguments (ES(n) from ES(n') via a move).
first_step: Build the graph for n ≤ 10⁴ and study components, degree distribution, and whether each prime connects to a smaller n by a short path.

title: Absorption method (Ringel, Erdős–Faber–Lovász): approximate structure + absorber ⇒ exact
connection: Combinatorial ∀n∃ conjectures were solved by building most of the object randomly and absorbing the leftovers. ES analogue: '4/p − (a cheap unit fraction) has a 2-term decomposition' succeeds for almost all choices; the absorber is the freedom in x.
why: Forces the question: is there an 'absorbing' set of x values (depending on p only through simple data) guaranteed to contain a good one?
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁸ find the minimal set X(p) of x-values (in terms of p mod small numbers) that always contains a working x; test stability.

title: Erdős's covering argument for prime plus powers of two
connection: The complement of n=p+2^k is controlled by congruence covering phenomena, resembling ES's finite congruence cover (F03) and thin-family unions (F34).
why: Covering congruences are a direct combinatorial mechanism for proving either coverage or obstruction, relevant to ES's certificate-line cover.
first_step: Write the covering congruence system in the Erdős argument and test whether ES failed primes have a finite modular covering explanation.
refs: P. Erdős, On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems, Summa Brasil. Math. 2 (1950) 113–123

title: Graceful tree conjecture: infinite families and absorption
connection: Graceful labeling shares F01,F05w,F23,F34: a universal finite-graph existence problem, many verified cases/families, and proof strategies that cover large classes. ES likewise needs an infinite union of thin certificate families.
why: The absorption method may suggest how to ensure a partial family cover can absorb leftover objects rather than merely prove density.
first_step: Read an absorption proof for a tree labeling result and abstract its ‘leave’ and absorber; formulate analogous objects as uncovered ES prime classes and certificate families.

title: Sandpile recurrence: finite states and critical group invariants
connection: Chip-firing/sandpile questions share F18w,F23,F32: reachability under local moves has finite-state invariants and short move-sequence certificates. ES matrix-word reachability offers a similar state-transition viewpoint.
why: Critical-group or modular invariants could cheaply eliminate impossible ES parameter words or classify search states.
first_step: Model ES matrix generators modulo m as a finite directed state graph and compare its conserved quantities with sandpile group invariants.

title: Tiling problems: local rules and global periodic witnesses
connection: Tiling existence shares F01,F03,F23,F32: local compatibility constraints must yield a global object, finite patches provide certificates, and computational searches test instances. ES similarly combines local congruences with a global positive integral witness.
why: Compactness/patching arguments can distinguish local consistency from global realizability, mirroring ES’s local-global gap.
first_step: Choose a concrete Wang-tile undecidability example and compare its local-to-global obstruction with ES’s local solubility; do not assume the techniques transfer absent a finite-state reduction.

title: Sum-product estimates for reciprocal sets
connection: Reciprocal additive equations share F12, F22, F33 and couple additive structure to multiplication of denominators.
why: Incidence bounds may quantify how many distinct reciprocal sums a structured denominator set can generate.
first_step: Apply an incidence bound to the sets {1/a} and {1/b+1/c} for bounded denominator ranges and compare with required p-scale.

title: Additive combinatorics of reciprocal residues
connection: Reciprocal residue sets share F10, F22, F33, where modular inverses combine additively to hit a target residue.
why: Sumset expansion could show that allowed denominator residues cannot avoid all ES target configurations.
first_step: For a prime modulus, compute restricted reciprocal sumsets from the ES denominator conditions and test known sum-product expansion bounds.

title: Graph connectivity of Diophantine representations
connection: Representation graphs share F14, F38, F39: vertices are solutions and local transformations connect them.
why: If each nonempty fibre has a canonical connected component, induction or descent might extend from a set of seeds.
first_step: Construct the ES witness graph under coordinate swaps and Vieta moves for small primes, then determine whether graph invariants suggest a general connectivity lemma.

title: Graph-theoretic reformulation: bipartite 'divisor graph' between levels C and primes p; (★) ⟺ no isolated prime vertex
connection: Make a bipartite graph with an edge (C, p) when R_C(p) > 0 ((★) divisor form at level C). (★)(p) ⟺ p has degree ≥ 1 — false at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰, so an ES version must add edges from other lines (e.g. the b = 1 line). Degree distribution ≍ Poisson(log²p) heuristically.
why: Graph tools (expansion, Hall-type conditions, random-graph thresholds for isolated vertices) give a different language for the lower tail (F04, F24).
first_step: Compute the bipartite graph for p ≤ 10⁷, C ≤ 10³; check the isolated-vertex threshold vs. random bipartite graphs with the same degree sequence.

title: Helfgott–Radziwiłł expansion of divisibility graphs
connection: Helfgott–Radziwiłł (2021) prove expansion of graphs on integers where n ~ n+p if p | n (prime p in a range), improving log-Chowla; ES witnesses are divisibility relations d | N with N in a p-tied family.
why: A divisibility-graph expander on {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} could transport 'some witness' along edges, the kind of local-to-global step ES lacks.
first_step: Build the graph on C ≤ 10^5 (fixed p) with edges C ~ C' if a common prime ℓ ≤ H divides both 4Cp+1 and 4C'p+1 and compute its spectral gap.
refs: Helfgott–Radziwiłł, Expansion, divisibility and parity, arXiv:2103.06853

title: Burgess-type bounds via Hanson–Petridis Stepanov method for structured residue sets
connection: Hanson–Petridis improve the Paley-graph clique bound to √(p/2)+1 using Stepanov's polynomial method; the repo found χ-product cliques sit in a QR coset and that |A|-only Hoffman/Huang bounds fail below (p−1)/2.
why: Stepanov's method uses more than |A| — multiplicative structure — which is what the χ-product clique obstruction asks for.
first_step: Apply the Hanson–Petridis polynomial to the repo's χ-product clique family and see whether it gives a bound depending on the generating set.
refs: Hanson–Petridis, Refined estimates concerning sumsets contained in the roots of unity, arXiv:1905.09134

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz for ES congruence certificates
connection: Alon's Nullstellensatz guarantees nonvanishing points in grids given a top-degree coefficient; mod-m versions of ES (local solubility with restricted coordinates) are polynomial non-vanishing questions over grids.
why: A grid-restricted solution mod many m simultaneously is a step toward ES with size-constrained denominators.
first_step: Write 'there exist x ∈ A, y ∈ B, z ∈ C with 4xyz ≡ n(xy+yz+zx) mod ℓ' and compute the relevant top coefficient to see when the Nullstellensatz applies.
refs: Alon, Combinatorial Nullstellensatz, Combin. Probab. Comput. 8 (1999)

title: Hypergraph containers for the set of possible ES failure sets
connection: Container lemmas (Balogh–Morris–Samotij, Saxton–Thomason) count independent sets in hypergraphs; the ES failure set is divisor-closed and must avoid every n with an identity — an independent set in an 'identity hypergraph'.
why: Containers bound how structured a failure set must be, a disproof-shape tool.
first_step: Count, for n ≤ 10^4 restricted to Mordell-hard residues, the number of divisor-closed sets avoiding identity coverage up to modulus M.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0075] Define the hypergraph on [N] whose edges are sets forced by multiplicativity and identities; compute container counts for N = 10^4.
refs: Balogh–Morris–Samotij, Independent sets in hypergraphs, JAMS 28 (2015)

title: Moreira monochromatic {x, x+y, xy} and Hindman sums/products (OAI 164)
connection: Moreira (Annals 2017) found monochromatic {x, x+y, xy}; OAI 164 claims Hindman's finite sums and products conjecture; ES mixes additive (4Cp+1) and multiplicative (divisor) operations.
why: Ergodic sum-product Ramsey results show additive and multiplicative structure can be forced together.
first_step: Phrase ES Type I as a configuration {p, C, 4Cp+1, d, (4Cp+1)/d} with additive and multiplicative relations and check whether it is a 'sum-product configuration' in Moreira's sense.
refs: Moreira, Monochromatic sums and products in N, Ann. Math. 185 (2017), arXiv:1605.01469

title: Mattheus–Verstraëte algebraic pseudorandom graphs (R(4,t)) from Hermitian unitals
connection: MV built optimal R(4,t) lower bounds from algebraic graphs over 𝔽_{q²}; ES-like 'sterile' residue structures are algebraic objects avoiding configurations.
why: Suggests constructing explicit algebraic sterile structures as candidates for counterexample-shape tests.
first_step: Check whether the repo's sterile residue patterns (STERILE_EXPLICIT.md) define an algebraic graph with Hermitian-unital-like incidence.
refs: Mattheus–Verstraëte, The asymptotics of r(4,t), arXiv:2306.04007

title: Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava interlacing families: existence of one good member
connection: MSS proved bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree exist by showing the expected characteristic polynomial's root bounds the root of some member (interlacing families); ES needs one good member (certificate) among a family.
why: Interlacing gives existence beyond first-moment counting when the quantity is a polynomial root — an unusual existence mechanism worth checking for ES polynomial encodings.
first_step: Encode ES certificates at p as roots/zeros of a family of real-rooted polynomials (e.g. via the lattice L_ρ's theta function restricted to a line) and test interlacing.
refs: Marcus–Spielman–Srivastava, Interlacing families I: bipartite Ramanujan graphs of all degrees, Ann. Math. 182 (2015), arXiv:1304.4132

title: Weighted dilation graphs / smooth shifted primes (OAI 'Weighted dilation graphs', claimed)
connection: The OAI paper claims x^{1−o(1)} primes p ∈ (2x,5x] with p−1 being x^δ-smooth via weighted dilation graphs; ES slices benefit from smooth N_e (many small generators).
why: Smooth shifted primes in abundance give structured slices; the dilation-graph technique is a new combinatorial counting tool.
first_step: Read the dilation-graph construction; test whether it can produce primes p with a smooth slice N_e for some small e.

title: Dias da Silva–Hamidoune restricted sumsets for distinct-factor products
connection: Erdős–Heilbronn (Dias da Silva–Hamidoune): |h^∧A| ≥ min(p, h|A| − h² + 1) for restricted h-fold sums in ℤ/p; ES uses products of distinct prime factors (restricted products).
why: Exact lower bounds for restricted product sets in cyclic groups of prime order (take discrete logs mod e−1 when e−1 is prime-ish).
first_step: Compute restricted product set sizes of prime factors of N mod e and compare with the DdS–H bound.
refs: Dias da Silva–Hamidoune, Cyclic spaces for Grassmann derivatives and additive theory, Bull. LMS 26 (1994)

title: Lorentzian polynomials (Brändén–Huh) / log-concavity of certificate-count sequences
connection: Lorentzian polynomials prove log-concavity of combinatorial sequences (matroid independent sets, etc.); ES certificate counts by size class or by number of prime factors used form sequences whose log-concavity could constrain zeros.
why: Log-concavity + positive endpoints ⇒ no internal zeros: a positivity mechanism that is pointwise.
first_step: For hard primes, compute the sequence a_k = #certificates using C with ω(C) = k (or certificate size buckets) and test log-concavity; if robust, look for a Lorentzian generating polynomial.
refs: Brändén–Huh, Lorentzian polynomials, Ann. Math. 192 (2020), arXiv:1902.03719

title: Adiprasito–Huh–Katz Hodge theory for matroids: positivity from combinatorial Hodge–Riemann
connection: AHK proved log-concavity (Rota/Heron/Welsh) via Hodge–Riemann relations on matroid Chow rings; U_n in reciprocal coordinates is a hyperplane-arrangement object (matroid of {u,v,w,u+v+w}).
why: Matroid Hodge theory gives positivity of combinatorial invariants of the arrangement; whether any ES count is such an invariant is the question.
first_step: Compute the characteristic polynomial / Chow ring of the arrangement for U_n and check whether any coefficient relates to solution counts (likely not; record).
refs: Adiprasito–Huh–Katz, Hodge theory for combinatorial geometries, Ann. Math. 188 (2018)

title: Ihara zeta / non-backtracking spectra of ES certificate graphs
connection: Ihara zeta functions encode cycle structure and Ramanujan property of graphs; the bipartite graph (C-values) ↔ (primes dividing 4Cp+1) at fixed p is a natural graph.
why: Spectral gap of this bipartite graph controls how dependent certificates are (Janson Δ).
first_step: Build the bipartite graph at a hard prime for C ≤ 10^4 and compute its non-backtracking spectrum.

title: Koukoulopoulos–Maynard GCD graphs for I3 overlaps across t
connection: I3 events for different t at fixed n share prime factors through gcd(tn+1, t′n+1) | (t−t′)… structure; GCD graphs quantify such overlaps.
why: Second-moment control at fixed n over t is the key missing step; GCD-graph compression is designed for that.
first_step: Compute gcd(tn+1, t′n+1) statistics for t,t′ ≤ 100 at the hardest I3 n values.

title: ES₅ as a sandpile-group pairing condition on a 4-vertex fan multigraph
connection: The chain matrix M = [[v,−1,0],[−1,t,−1],[0,−1,u]] is the reduced Laplacian of the multigraph: path a–b–c plus a sink s joined to a, b, c by v−1, t−2, u−1 parallel edges. It has det M = tuv−u−v = p spanning trees, a cyclic sandpile group ℤ/p, and its discriminant (monodromy) pairing has self-pairing (M⁻¹)₁₁ = A/p. So ES₅(p) (∃ t,u,v ≥ 2, tuv−u−v = p, (A/p) = −1 with A = tu−1; sufficient for ES(p)) ⇔ some fan multigraph of this shape with p spanning trees has a sandpile pairing in the non-square class.
why: Sandpile groups with their pairings are a mature field (Lorenzini, Shokrieh, Bosch–Lorenzini) with classification results for pairings on cyclic critical groups; this gives ES₅ a purely graph-theoretic statement.
first_step: Script: for p ≡ 1 (4) < 10⁵, enumerate all graphs on ≤ 5 vertices with p spanning trees and record which pairing classes occur; is the non-square class reached by 4-vertex fans exactly when ES₅(p) holds, and always by 5-vertex graphs?
refs: arXiv:2311.06367 (Lorenzini, The critical polynomial of a graph)

title: Relaxing the fan: which pairing classes occur among graphs with p spanning trees and k vertices
connection: Generalise item 1: the graph-theoretic analogue of 'ES with more terms' is 'some graph with ≤ k vertices and τ(G) = p has a non-square sandpile pairing'. ES₅ is the k = 4 fan case. (Not via cycles/trees: a tree has trivial critical group, and C_p has pairing class −1/p, which is a square for p ≡ 1 (4). For large k a non-square class should come from longer chains, i.e. from λ(p) ≤ k − 1, which is known for k ≫ log p.)
why: Gives a ladder of relaxations parametrised by vertex count, with a known extremal theory for τ(G) values (Sedláček's α(n)); the threshold k(p) at which the non-square pairing first appears is a new invariant to compare with λ(p).
first_step: Compute k*(p) = least vertex count with a non-square pairing and τ = p, for p < 10⁴; compare with λ(p) and with Stong/Azarija–Škrekovski bounds for α(p).
refs: Stong, Minimal graphs with a prescribed number of spanning trees, Australas. J. Combin. 82 (2022)

title: Modular spanning-tree realisation (Alon–Bucić–Gishboliner) as a model for the sign condition
connection: Alon–Bucić–Gishboliner show every residue u mod N is τ(G) mod N for some planar G on O(log N) vertices. ES₅ is a 'τ(G) = p exactly and pairing class prescribed' statement on 4 vertices.
why: Their short combinatorial proofs control τ(G) modulo N with few vertices; a version controlling the pairing class (a mod-p quadratic datum) would be a graph-theoretic analogue of an ES-type sign theorem.
first_step: Read arXiv:2503.23648; check whether their gadgets allow simultaneous control of τ(G) and the square class of the sandpile pairing.

title: Idoneal numbers in spanning-tree extremal problems vs U(n)/I3 sporadic lists
connection: Azarija–Škrekovski: α(n) ≤ (n+4)/3 iff n ∉ {3,4,5,6,7,9,10,13,18,22}, a subset of Euler's idoneal numbers. U(n)/I3 have finite sporadic failure lists for tuv−u−v representations, also continuant/spanning-tree statements.
why: The appearance of idoneal numbers (class-group exponent ≤ 2) in a spanning-tree problem suggests the U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} might have a class-group characterisation.
first_step: Compute the class groups Cl(−4n), Cl(−n) for the U(n) sporadics and for I3 failures; test exponent-2 / genus-one patterns.

title: Sylver coinage / numerical-semigroup games on the forest's Frobenius classes
connection: The forest edge relation uv | p+u+v identifies p as a 'Frobenius-shadow' point of ⟨u,v⟩. Conway's Sylver coinage is a game whose positions are numerical semigroups; P-positions are related to Frobenius data.
why: Game positions give a different combinatorial calculus on pairs (u,v); an ES-relevant invariant might appear as a Sprague–Grundy value. Low prior but not meaningless.
first_step: Compute Sprague–Grundy-type data for two-generator Sylver positions ⟨u,v⟩ with uv | p+u+v; look for any correlation with (uv/p).

title: Kirchhoff/Brooks–Smith–Stone–Tutte: squared rectangles from planar networks with p spanning trees
connection: A planar network with τ = p spanning trees gives a rectangle tiled by squares with sides of total scale p (BSST). The fan graph of item 1 is planar, so ES₅ gives a squared rectangle of a specific shape whose aspect ratio encodes the resistance A/p.
why: Squared-rectangle theory has a 'reduced side' (= τ) and aspect ratios = resistances. ES₅ becomes: some 4-vertex-network squared rectangle with reduced side p has aspect class non-residue.
first_step: Compute BSST rectangles for the fan networks at small p; check whether the aspect-ratio numerator class is visible geometrically (e.g. via tile parity).

title: Domino/strip tilings counted by continuants with a parity weight
connection: Positive continuants count tilings of a strip by monominoes and dominoes with weights. The negative continuant K(v,t,u) = tuv−u−v is a signed count, equivalently det of the chain matrix as a weighted path-matching count. The ES sign is the class of the cofactor.
why: Tiling enumeration has transfer-matrix and involution machinery. A sign-reversing involution on tilings might isolate a non-residue cofactor.
first_step: Write tuv−u−v and tu−1 as tiling counts of a 3-cell strip with weights; look for a sign-reversing involution whose fixed points carry the class of tu−1 mod p.
refs: Benjamin–Quinn, Proofs that Really Count (continuants ch. 4)

title: Matrix-tree theorem with signed/twisted weights: the ES sign as a determinant of a twisted Laplacian
connection: (A/p) for the fan graph equals the Legendre symbol of a principal cofactor of the reduced Laplacian M (principal cofactors of the full Laplacian all equal p). Twisted Laplacians (connection Laplacians with ℤ/2 or ℤ/4 holonomy) compute signed spanning-forest counts (Kenyon's cycle-rooted spanning forests).
why: Kenyon's vector-bundle Laplacian theory computes topological invariants of forests via determinants. A ℤ/4 connection might encode the slot-lemma condition '4 | some pentagon entry'.
first_step: Put a ℤ/4 connection on the fan graph; compute det of the connection Laplacian and compare with the slot-lemma indicator over all words for p < 1000.
refs: Kenyon, Spanning forests and the vector bundle Laplacian (Ann. Probab. 2011)

title: Hoffman/spectral bound on the forest F_p with Legendre colouring (bichromatic edge existence)
connection: ES₅ for p ≡ 1 (8) ⇔ the word forest F_p has a bichromatic edge under v ↦ (v/p). Spectral graph theory bounds the size of monochromatic (independent-type) sets via eigenvalues.
why: It is the textbook first tool for 'every 2-colouring with given class sizes has a bichromatic edge'. The Legendre colouring has known sizes inside intervals (Burgess), but F_p is sparse.
first_step: Compute the spectrum of F_p for p < 10⁴; compare λ_max/λ_min with the size of the QR set inside vertices to see if Hoffman-type bounds are anywhere near.

title: Isoperimetry/expansion of the forest components vs character-sum smoothness
connection: If the component of 1 in F_p has edge expansion h and contains a QNR, then a bichromatic edge exists. Combinatorial expansion of an arithmetic forest is a graph-theory question.
why: 'The component containing 1 reaches a QNR' is a sufficient (not necessary) condition for ES₅, the arithmetic analogue of a percolation/connectivity statement. FRONTIER §3 records that under Dickson it fails infinitely often (e.g. p = 409 has a monochromatic component of 1 but a negative word (15,4,7)).
first_step: Compute the component sizes of F_p and the least QNR inside the component of 1, for p < 10⁶.

title: ℤ/2 gauge field on F_p plus multiplicative edges: the Legendre colouring as a flat connection
connection: F_p is a forest, so its own critical group is trivial and colourings carry no holonomy. Adding 'multiplicative' edges u ~ qu (q a small prime, weight (q/p)) creates cycles. The Legendre colouring is then a ℤ/2 gauge configuration that is flat around every cycle by multiplicativity, and ES₅ failure means it is also constant along every forest edge.
why: Speculative: combining the forest's divisibility edges with multiplicative edges might force a contradiction for a flat ℤ/2 connection that is trivial on forest edges, i.e. a global consistency obstruction that a single forest cannot carry.
first_step: Build the augmented graph for p < 2000 (forest + edges u ~ 2u, 3u, 5u); compute the space of ℤ/2 colourings that are multiplicative on the added edges and constant on forest edges, and its dimension.

title: Frieze patterns with coefficients (Cuntz–Holm–Jørgensen) for boundary (1,1,1,1,N)
connection: CHJ develop friezes with coefficients and prove finiteness: for given boundary there are finitely many friezes with entries in a discrete set. They also obtain them by cutting subpolygons out of triangulated polygons. ES₅ words are exactly the positive integral friezes of the pentagon with boundary (1,1,1,1,N) (FRIEZE_ES).
why: Their 'cutting out subpolygons from Conway–Coxeter friezes' construction could realise each ES₅ word inside a classical triangulation of an (N+…)-gon, giving a triangulation model of the sign.
first_step: Read arXiv:1909.02332 §§3–5. Represent each word for p < 200 as a cut-out from a Conway–Coxeter frieze and check whether the sign (4 | quiddity entry) is visible on the triangulation.

title: Conway–Coxeter triangulation count with a mod-4 marked quiddity entry
connection: Classical friezes ↔ triangulations (Conway–Coxeter). The slot lemma says the ES sign is −1 iff 4 divides one of the five pentagon entries (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1). So ES₅ asks for a frieze with coefficients having an entry ≡ 0 (mod 4).
why: 'Some quiddity entry ≡ 0 mod 4' is a reduction-mod-4 condition, and friezes over ℤ/4 (or SL₂(ℤ/4) Farey complexes) are finite objects with full classifications.
first_step: Enumerate the mod-4 reductions of all positive words for p < 10⁵ and record which mod-4 frieze types occur per p; compare with Morier-Genoud's counts of friezes over finite rings.
refs: Morier-Genoud, Counting Coxeter's friezes over a finite field via moduli spaces (check arXiv id)

title: Tropical frieze / tropicalisation of the pentagon-with-coefficient
connection: Replacing (×,+) by (+,max) gives a tropical frieze: 2-adic valuations of the pentagon entries satisfy the tropical Ptolemy relations only as inequalities (v₂(a+b) ≥ min, with equality unless there is cancellation, e.g. 1 + 1 = 2), so they give tropical constraints, not a tropical frieze. The slot lemma condition is a 2-adic valuation event (v₂(entry) ≥ 2).
why: Tropical friezes are piecewise-linear and fully classifiable, so they might give a necessary-and-sufficient 2-adic shape of sign-(−1) words.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic valuation vectors (v₂ of the 5 entries) of all words for p < 10⁵ and the allowed tropical patterns; check whether every p has a pattern with some v₂ ≥ 2.

title: Laurent phenomenon: all frieze entries as Laurent polynomials in an initial seed (c, m) with coefficient N
connection: In a cluster algebra with frozen N, every entry is a Laurent polynomial in an initial cluster. ES words are integrality (positivity) points of these Laurent polynomials, so ES₅ is an 'integer specialisation of a cluster algebra' problem.
why: The theory of integer points of cluster varieties (positivity, theta bases, Fock–Goncharov) is native here, and may give parametrisations of all words by a seed.
first_step: Write the five entries as Laurent polynomials in (c,m) with N; the integrality condition is (cm−1) | (N + c). Record that the frieze reproduces the hyperbola/divisor condition, and check whether any other seed gives a different divisor condition.

title: SL₂-tilings (Bergeron–Reutenauer) containing a row of five with boundary N
connection: SL₂-tilings are infinite arrays of 2×2 minors 1; friezes are bounded tilings. A word gives a finite SL₂-pattern; Bergeron–Reutenauer parametrise tilings by bi-infinite paths in the Farey graph.
why: It turns words into Farey-graph path pairs, where the ES sign might be a holonomy in SL₂(ℤ/4) along the path pair (SVZ already looked at mod-4 contractibility).
first_step: Compute the Bergeron–Reutenauer path pair of each word; check whether the mod-4 holonomy distinguishes signs.
refs: Bergeron–Reutenauer, SL_k-tilings of the plane (Illinois J. 2010)

title: Positive points of cluster varieties ↔ tropical points (Fock–Goncharov duality) for the ES frieze
connection: Fock–Goncharov: positive-integer tropical points of a cluster X-variety parametrise a canonical basis of the dual A-variety. ES words are positive integer points of an A-type frieze variety with coefficient.
why: If ES words were tropical points of a dual variety, existence would become 'a certain polyhedral cone contains an integer point', which is linear.
first_step: Identify the dual (X-variety) of the A₂-with-coefficient frieze variety; compute its tropical points relevant to N; check whether the A-integer points (words) are in bijection with them.
refs: Fock–Goncharov, Cluster ensembles, quantization and the dilogarithm (2009)

title: Quiver representations of A₂ with dimension-vector data equal to a word
connection: Friezes of type A_n categorify via Caldero–Chapoton maps on cluster categories of A_n. Frieze entries are Euler characteristics of quiver Grassmannians. Coefficients correspond to frozen vertices (Frobenius categories).
why: Categorification gives representation-theoretic meaning to every entry, so 'entry ≡ 0 mod 4' becomes 'Euler characteristic of a quiver Grassmannian ≡ 0 mod 4'.
first_step: Find the Frobenius 2-CY category categorifying friezes with coefficients (Holm–Jørgensen line of work), and identify which objects give entries t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1.

title: Sum-product / Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin for the set S_L(p) as L grows
connection: S_L(p) = {A : r(p/A) ≤ L} grows like p^{c(L)} for L ≫ log p. Sum-product theory says sets of size p^δ generate F_p in bounded steps. ES₅ fixes L = 3, where |S₃| ≈ log²p.
why: It is the native additive-combinatorics frame for why L = 3 is hard (polylog sets have no sum-product leverage) and where L-ladders become easy.
first_step: Tabulate |S_L(p)| and the least L with S_L(p) ⊄ QR for p < 10⁶ (this is λ(p)); fit L_min growth.

title: Percolation on the forest F_p: giant component reaching a QNR
connection: If F_p behaves like a random graph above the percolation threshold, the component of 1 is giant and contains a QNR. ES₅ (p ≡ 1 mod 8) follows from 'the component of 1 contains a QNR'.
why: Percolation-native: thresholds are sharp, and arithmetic graphs (divisor graphs) have percolation results (e.g. random divisor graphs). The forest might be supercritical in a window of small vertices.
first_step: Compute the degree distribution and component structure of F_p restricted to vertices ≤ X for p < 10⁷; locate the effective percolation threshold.

title: Maker–Breaker / Erdős–Selfridge criterion for covering-system strategies
connection: View 'adversary chooses p's residues prime by prime, prover covers with certificates' as a Maker–Breaker game on a hypergraph of congruence certificates. The Erdős–Selfridge criterion Σ 2^{−|e|} < 1/2 gives Breaker (adversary) a win.
why: It turns B1 (no finite covering) into a game-theory calculation and might quantify how large the certificate hypergraph must be for a covering, compared with the actual size.
first_step: Compute the Erdős–Selfridge potential of the certificate hypergraph up to level C₀ (edges = residue-class conditions on p); see where it crosses 1/2.

title: Garsia–Milne involution principle for a bijective ES-count identity
connection: The involution principle builds a bijection from two sign-reversing involutions. If N₋(p) = (count of a simple positive set) − (count of another) via explicit involutions, Garsia–Milne yields a bijection and hence positivity whenever the simple set is bigger.
why: It is the enumerative-combinatorics native machine for turning signed identities into injections. Positivity of ES would follow from an injection from a set of known size ≥ 1.
first_step: Look for any signed identity for N₋ (SIGN_IDENTITY lists the known ones); check whether its terms are counts of explicit finite sets amenable to involutions.

title: Kasteleyn/Pfaffian orientations: ES count as a Pfaffian of a skew matrix built from p
connection: Perfect matchings of planar graphs are Pfaffians. Windmill-type 'odd number of fixed points' arguments are mod-2 Pfaffian/determinant arguments. A planar graph G_p with ES certificates as matchings would give #certificates = |Pf(K_p)|.
why: Exact Pfaffian formulas give closed-form counts, and nonvanishing of a determinant is checkable algebraically (e.g. via its value mod a prime).
first_step: Attempt to realise the forest F_p's edges or the words as perfect matchings of a planar graph; compute det mod 2 for small p.

title: Sperner / KKM / Tucker lemmas for a labelled triangulation whose 'rainbow cell' is a certificate
connection: Sperner's lemma gives an odd number of fully labelled simplices. If the triangle {x+y+z = const} or the (u,v) quadrant can be triangulated with labels from p-arithmetic (e.g. Legendre symbols and divisibility), a rainbow cell might encode a word with the right sign.
why: It is the combinatorial-topology native parity engine with geometric flexibility. The forest bichromatic-edge statement is already a 1-dimensional Sperner-type statement (path from QR to QNR has a bichromatic edge).
first_step: Write the 1-D Sperner argument behind H4/forest bichromatic edges explicitly; then look for a 2-D labelling that encodes the extra divisibility.

title: Lorenzini's critical-polynomial question (W) and the A₃ graph: I3 as a sandpile statement
connection: LORENZINI_W: (W) asks that every n outside a finite set is xyz − x − z (x,y,z ≥ 2), which comes from critical groups of A₃-type graphs. I3 (t,u,v ≥ 3) is a strengthening.
why: This is the graph-theory native home of I3. Lorenzini's and Wang–Lu's density-1 results are its nearest theorems.
first_step: Check Wang–Lu (EJC 2026) methods for density 1 and whether they extend to the I3 lower bound t,u,v ≥ 3 (repo has an unconditional rate).
refs: Wang–Lu, The critical polynomials of simple connected graphs, EJC 33(3) (2026)

title: Tutte polynomial of the fan graph: evaluations beyond T(1,1) = p
connection: The fan multigraph's Tutte polynomial T(x,y) has T(1,1) = p. Other evaluations count forests, acyclic orientations, recurrent sandpile levels (Merino) and, via Thistlethwaite, the Jones polynomial of the associated alternating link.
why: It is a single polynomial carrying graph, sandpile and knot data. The ES sign might be an evaluation (e.g. T(−1,−1) or a root-of-unity value).
first_step: Compute T(x,y) symbolically for the fan in terms of (t,u,v) and evaluate at small roots of unity; correlate with the slot-lemma sign.

title: Pentagon identity of the dilogarithm on the coefficient-N pentagon
connection: The Rogers dilogarithm satisfies the 5-term relation along A₂ mutations: Σ L(X_i/(1+X_i)) = π²/2 on the positive real locus. With frozen coefficient N the relation acquires N-dependent terms. Words give rational points.
why: Dilogarithm identities encode K₂/Bloch-group data of the points. For rational points, Bloch-group elements are torsion, which gives exact identities; the sign might appear as a torsion class.
first_step: Compute Σ L over the five X-coordinates of each word for p < 100 numerically; look for a pattern in N and in the sign.

title: Multiplicative generation of F_p^* by forest edge products
connection: A = (p+u)/v ≡ u/v (mod p), so (A/p) = (uv/p) on forest edges. ES₅ fails ⇒ every edge product uv lies in the QR subgroup ⇒ the group generated by edge products is ≠ F_p^*. So ES₅(p) ⇐ 'edge products generate F_p^*'.
why: Generation of (ℤ/q)^× by small structured sets is now proved for almost all q (Klurman–Shparlinski–Teräväinen). Edge products are small integers with a divisibility constraint; this links ES₅ to the 'small sets generate' literature.
first_step: Compute the index of ⟨uv : (u,v) edge of F_p, u,v ≤ X⟩ in F_p^* as X grows, p < 10⁶; compare the least X needed with the least QNR.

title: Brown–Rödl partition regularity of 1/x + 1/y = 1/z and inhomogeneous colourings
connection: Brown–Rödl: in every finite colouring of ℕ the equation 1/x + 1/y = 1/z has a monochromatic solution. Croot: 1 = Σ 1/x_i monochromatic. ES is inhomogeneous (4/n), but 'colour n by ES status' and look for monochromatic structures.
why: Ramsey-theory native: a hypothetical ES-failure set F cannot contain configurations forced by partition regularity of related equations, which gives structural constraints on F.
first_step: Find equations E with E(n₁,…) ∧ ES(n₁) ∧ … ⇒ ES(n_k) (transport laws) and combine them with partition regularity to constrain F's structure.
refs: Brown–Rödl, Monochromatic solutions to equations with unit fractions (Bull. Austral. Math. Soc. 1991)

title: Gcd structure across levels: gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) | 4(C′−C)·… as a coupling axiom
connection: For two levels, gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) divides C′(4Cp+1) − C(4C′p+1) = C′ − C. So prime factors are shared between levels only through C′ − C. This is the exact coupling of the family {4Cp+1}.
why: This 'gcd-coupling' is the arithmetic analogue of the dependency graph in LLL/Janson. Any pointwise argument across levels must exploit it.
first_step: Build the level-dependency hypergraph for p via shared primes q | C′ − C, and test whether failure patterns in data are explained by it.

title: Configuration-model random graph for F_p with the divisor-degree sequence
connection: Model F_p as a random graph with the same degree sequence (degrees = numbers of valid partners). Component-size predictions (Molloy–Reed criterion) show whether the component of 1 should be giant.
why: It gives a quantitative null model for forest connectivity, and deviations would show the arithmetic is non-random in a usable way.
first_step: Compute the degree sequence of F_p and the Molloy–Reed quantity Σ d(d−2); compare predicted and actual component sizes for p < 10⁶.

title: Temperley bijection: ES₅ fan ↔ a planar bipartite graph with exactly p perfect matchings
connection: Temperley's bijection maps spanning trees of a planar graph G to perfect matchings of a derived bipartite graph. The fan multigraph with τ = p therefore yields a planar bipartite graph with p dimer configurations; Kasteleyn matrices compute them as determinants, and height functions carry signs.
why: Dimer models have height functions and Kasteleyn signs; the ES sign (pairing class) might be a dimer observable, e.g. the parity of height-function flux around a face.
first_step: Construct the Temperley graph of the fan for small words and compute the Kasteleyn matrix; test whether a height-function statistic mod 2 matches the slot-lemma sign.

title: Conway–Coxeter count analogue: number of positive friezes with boundary (1,1,1,1,N) as an arithmetic function of N
connection: Classical friezes of the n-gon are counted by Catalan numbers. With coefficient N on one side, the number of positive integral pentagon friezes is an arithmetic function F(N) (≈ number of words incl. boundary words ≍ log²N). ES₅ refines it by the sign.
why: Generating functions of frieze counts with coefficients might be more structured (e.g. in terms of divisor functions or class numbers) than word counts, with a combinatorial (triangulation) interpretation via CHJ.
first_step: Compute F(N) and F₋(N) for N < 10⁵; search OEIS and fit to divisor-function combinations.

title: Graph structure on certificates of a fixed p
connection: BGS/Chen study the connectivity of a graph on solutions. Define moves between ES certificates of the same p (change C keeping u, swap roles of u/B, Type I↔II transforms) and study components; 'one certificate ⇒ many' plus a counting congruence on component sizes might exclude zero.
why: Even if ES is not about connectivity, component structure can produce congruences (as in Chen).
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ build the move graph on all ES solutions and record component sizes; look for divisibility patterns.
refs: arXiv:2011.12940 (Chen, Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples, Ann. Math. 2024)

title: Slice-rank bounds for certificate-avoiding exponent sets
connection: Croot–Lev–Pach/Ellenberg–Gijswijt bound sets avoiding x + y + z = 0 via slice rank. ES failure constrains the exponent vectors (mod 2, or in the character group) of prime factors of N_e so that no ±1 combination hits the class of −1: a linear-avoidance condition in a 2-group quotient of (ℤ/e)*. Slice-rank-type bounds limit such sets.
why: Gives quantitative 'avoidance is rare' statements in elementary abelian quotients of (ℤ/e)*.
first_step: For e with (ℤ/e)*/squares ≅ F₂^r, formulate the avoidance condition on the F₂-vectors of prime factors and compute the maximal avoiding sets for small r.
refs: arXiv:1605.01506 (Croot-Lev-Pach, Progression-free sets in Z_4^n are exponentially small)

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz on the trial form
connection: Alon's nullstellensatz proves existence of a nonvanishing point in a grid. R(p)/2 = #{d : 4c_d(p) | d + 1, d² ≤ 4c_d(p)p + 1}: encode 'no d in a grid of structured values works' as a polynomial vanishing on a product set, and look for a monomial whose coefficient is nonzero.
why: A purely algebraic existence argument; most likely to work in a finite-field shadow (mod q) of the problem, giving at least a structural lemma.
first_step: Formulate the mod-q shadow: for prime q, find (u, C) ∈ S₁ × S₂ (small sets) with 4uC − 1 ≡ 0 and p + u ≡ 0 (mod q); test the nullstellensatz coefficient condition.

title: Reiher's double counting: subsequences of fixed length with prescribed sum
connection: Reiher combined Chevalley–Warning with counting of subsequences of each length. ES analogue: count divisors of N of each 'length' (number of prime factors) in each class mod 4C; parity/divisibility constraints between lengths might force the class −1 to be hit.
why: Fine-grained counts by number of prime factors carry more structure than the total divisor-class set.
first_step: For N = 4Cp+1 with ω(N) ≥ 4, compute the table (k, class) ↦ #{divisors with k prime factors in class}, and look for identities mod 2 or mod 3.

title: Extremal vs non-extremal split for ES
connection: EFL/Ringel proofs split into 'extremal' configurations (handled by hand) and 'random-like' ones (absorption). ES: random-like p (character values balanced) vs extremal p (QR at many small primes; square-like mod large M); handle extremal p by forced-congruence arguments (least non-residue) and random-like p by second-moment counting.
why: Gives a concrete division of labour where each part may be tractable; the extremal side is close to the Burgess/least-non-residue world.
first_step: Define an extremality score E(p) (e.g. number of primes ℓ ≤ 100 with (p/ℓ) = 1) and examine how certificate counts depend on it.

title: Unavoidable configurations + discharging over levels
connection: Four colour theorem: every planar graph contains one of 633 reducible configurations (found by discharging). ES: define 'configurations' as local data (p mod small M, factorisation pattern of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ K); show by a discharging/averaging argument that every p contains one of a finite list, each of which forces a certificate.
why: B1's Thm M says bounded procedures follow formal runs at square-mimicking points, so the configuration list must include unbounded data; still the method gives a framework for structured case analysis.
first_step: Collect, for p ≤ 10⁸, the minimal 'certificate-forcing' local configurations and see whether a small set covers all p empirically.

title: Partial-colouring pigeonhole: collisions of near-certificates yield certificates
connection: Spencer/Beck: exponentially many colourings fall into few buckets, two collide, their difference is a good partial colouring. ES: generate many near-certificates for p (objects mapping to a small 'defect' space), pigeonhole two into the same bucket, and combine them (difference/quotient) into an exact certificate — the Pell/Dirichlet mechanism with an entropy count.
why: The entropy count tells exactly how many near-certificates are needed versus the bucket count; if near-certificates are power-many while buckets are polylog-many, collisions are guaranteed.
first_step: Identify a combination law (SL₂ quotients, divisor ratios) and a defect space; count near-certificates vs buckets for test p.
refs: Spencer, Trans. AMS 289 (1985) 679-706 (Six standard deviations suffice)

title: Dvir-type bound for certificate-free residue sets modulo q
connection: Dvir's polynomial argument shows Kakeya sets are large. Dual question for ES: how large can a set A of residues r mod q (q prime) be such that no r ∈ A admits a (★)-type certificate with parameters in a box (u, B, C ≤ Q)? A low-degree polynomial vanishing on A and its 'directions' could bound |A|.
why: Upper bounds on certificate-free residue sets mod q translate into 'most residues are covered' statements with explicit polynomial-method constants.
first_step: Compute certificate-free residue sets mod q for q ≤ 10⁴ and box sizes Q; compare their sizes with q·(1 − c) and check for algebraic structure (squares?).
refs: arXiv:0803.2336 (Dvir, On the size of Kakeya sets in finite fields)

title: Zero-sum over levels: among many levels, some combination of near-certificates is exact
connection: EGZ guarantees a zero-sum subsequence of prescribed length. ES near-certificates at different levels C carry 'defect classes' in groups (ℤ/4C)*; if defects lived in a common group, a zero-sum subsequence of defects could combine into an exact certificate (requires a combination law across levels).
why: Odd: needs a multiplicative combination law; but zero-sum theory exactly converts 'many near-misses' into 'one hit'.
first_step: Find a common quotient group for defects at levels C ≡ 0 (mod M) (e.g. (ℤ/M)*) and test whether products of near-certificates at different levels produce certificates at the lcm level.

title: Erdős–Selfridge distinct-small-parts mechanism for consecutive levels
connection: Erdős–Selfridge: writing consecutive factors as a_i·(power) forces the a_i to be distinct and small, contradiction by counting. ES failure forces each 4Cp+1 (C = 1, …, K) into a thin multiplicative set S_C; write 4Cp+1 = a_C·b_C with b_C the S_C-compatible part and look for a forced-distinctness/smallness contradiction among the a_C.
why: An elementary combinatorial mechanism for consecutive terms that might bite on the explicit sets S_C at small C.
first_step: For C ≤ 8 characterise S_C explicitly (e.g. S_1: all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4) and test numerically how small K can be such that no prime has 4Cp+1 ∈ S_C for all C ≤ K... (there are such primes for each K; record their density decay).

title: Instance transformation that preserves certificate existence but amplifies counts
connection: Reingold transformed every graph into an expander while preserving connectivity. ES: find a transformation p ↦ (structured object with power-many 'attempts') such that ES(p) ⟺ the object has a 'connected/nonzero' property that is robustly detectable (e.g. a spectral quantity), amplifying the polylog main term.
why: If the count can be amplified while preserving the zero/nonzero status, the polylog-main-term barrier (B2) changes character.
first_step: Look at the equivalence ES(p) ⟺ ∃e (e-slice form, Type I and Type II N's) and the implication (★)-level certificate ⇒ ES(p); build a graph on (e, divisors of N_e) whose connectivity property is equivalent to ES(p), and compute its spectral gap for small p.
refs: Reingold, J. ACM 55 (2008) Art. 17 (Undirected connectivity in log-space)

title: Fixed-length subproducts: ES with a prescribed number of prime factors in the divisor
connection: Kemnitz/Reiher control zero-sums of prescribed length. Refine ES: is there always a certificate whose divisor d has exactly k prime factors for some small k (e.g. k ≤ 2)? If 'k ≤ 2' holds empirically, ES reduces to a statement about prime pairs (q₁ q₂ ≡ −1 mod 4C) — a zero-sum of length 2.
why: A bounded-length version is much more structured (pairs of primes in classes) and amenable to sieve/character methods.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁸, record for each p the minimal Ω(d) over certificates; find primes requiring Ω(d) ≥ 3.

title: Recursive product constructions: certificates for p from certificates for pieces of 4Cp + 1
connection: Bose–Shrikhande–Parker built orthogonal Latin squares of composite orders from smaller ones. For ES, 4Cp + 1 = N₁N₂ (coprime): if N₁ has a divisor ≡ a (mod 4C) and N₂ one ≡ b with ab ≡ −1, the product is a certificate. Study 'recursive' constructions splitting N and combining class information from each piece.
why: Product constructions are the combinatorial counterpart of the Kneser/product-set items, with an explicit recursive structure.
first_step: For hard p, enumerate coprime splittings of 4Cp + 1 and compute the class sets of divisors of each piece; count combinations giving −1.

title: Surgery on near-certificates: local modifications that remove a single obstruction
connection: Perelman's surgery removes singularities and continues the flow. For a near-certificate at level C (a divisor d of 4Cp + 1 in a class ≠ −1), define 'surgeries' changing one prime factor (moving to another level C′ sharing that factor via CRT) and study whether repeated surgery reaches a certificate.
why: Gives a local-move graph on near-certificates across levels, linked by shared prime factors.
first_step: Build the graph (nodes: (C, d); edges: share a prime factor q, C ≡ C′ (mod q)) for small p and search paths to certificates.
refs: arXiv:math/0211159 (Perelman, The entropy formula for the Ricci flow)

title: Erdős multiplication-table problem ↔ number of distinct products in Type II parametrizations
connection: Ford's resolution of the multiplication-table problem counts distinct products ab ≤ x. ES Type II parameters generate integers as products; overlaps among products reduce effective tickets.
why: The multiplication-table constant (log x)^{−δ} is the same exponent as in divisors-in-intervals; ES heuristics should incorporate it.
first_step: Compute the overlap rate among Type II certificate products for fixed p and compare with Ford's constant.

title: ES in the max-denominator-minimizing world: optimal solutions and their arithmetic
connection: For each p choose the solution minimizing max(x,y,z). The optimal solution is a canonical object; its Type (I/II) and parameters form a function of p whose structure may be simpler than the full solution set.
why: A canonical solution map p ↦ s(p) could be guessed (e.g. 'smallest C with a certificate') and proved by showing the guess always works.
first_step: Compute s(p) for p ≤ 10^5; tabulate its type and parameters; look for a rule.

title: Union-of-slices world with a 'budget': ES restricted to the first B slices — false for each fixed B, but by how much?
connection: Each fixed set of B slices is a finite covering ⇒ fails on a positive-density set (square classes and more). The density of failures f(B) as B grows measures how fast ES's certificate supply converges.
why: f(B) → 0 is equivalent to Vaughan-type almost-all; its rate is a concrete function to compute and model (e.g. f(B) ≍ exp(−c√B)?).
first_step: Compute f(B) for B ≤ 200 using p < 10^7; fit decay.

title: Transfer: AGP-style construction for a disproof (many primes failing simultaneously)
connection: AGP build L with many primes q, q−1 | L. Dually, a counterexample search could build p with p ≡ prescribed residues mod many 4ad simultaneously (CRT) — avoiding all Type I APs up to a bound.
why: Covering-type disproofs fail for ES (failures can't fill an AP), but CRT-constructed 'avoiders' up to a bound X show how many families can be dodged simultaneously; prime in the CRT class then by Linnik.
first_step: Compute the density of residue classes mod lcm{4ad : ad ≤ X} avoiding all Type I/II APs; how fast does it decay with X? (Gives an 'avoidance exponent'.)

title: Transfer: Two-squares decomposition p = a² + b² as a forced object
connection: p ≡ 1 mod 4 has a unique a² + b²; check whether 4/p has certificates expressible in a, b (e.g. via (a ± b), a² − b², ab).
why: If a fixed finite set of polynomial-in-(a,b) formulas solved ES, it would bypass Mordell–Schinzel (those are polynomial in p, not in a,b).
first_step: For p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^6, test whether some x ∈ {a, b, a+b, a−b, ab, a²−b², …}·small multiples gives 4/p − 1/x a 2-term fraction (Stewart test).

title: Greedy set-cover growth of primes by ES certificate families
connection: Order Type I/II families (by modulus) and compute the minimum number of families needed to cover all primes ≡ 1 mod 24 up to x. Finite coverings are impossible (B1); the growth rate (log x? log² x?) measures 'how infinite' ES's covering is.
why: Compare with covering systems (finite) and with p + 2^k (no covering of the complement). A slow (≈ log x) growth would suggest a structured infinite covering.
first_step: Implement greedy set cover over families with modulus ≤ M for primes ≤ 10^7; plot cover size vs x.

title: AP-avoidance density: CRT classes dodging all Type I families with ad ≤ X
connection: Compute the density δ(X) of residue classes (coprime, ≡ 1 mod 24) that avoid every Type I AP −f mod 4ad with ad ≤ X. ES ⇔ no prime survives all X; the decay rate of δ(X) is the 'covering strength'.
why: If δ(X) decays like exp(−c log² X) it matches Vaughan's exceptional set; slower decay would leave room for many CRT-constructed near-counterexamples.
first_step: Monte Carlo over random large residues, X = 10..2000; fit log δ vs log X.

title: Prediction: under GRH the 'sign layer' reaches n(p) ≤ 2 log² p, so if s(p) were a function of n(p) alone ES would follow — the data say it is not alone
connection: Bach's bound makes character patterns of p escape square-like behaviour by ℓ ≈ 2 log² p. If ES-hardness were controlled only by n(p) (plus bounded noise), a GRH-conditional pointwise argument would exist. The observed n(p) = 17 record with s = 2814 shows extra (class-layer) difficulty — consistent with the campaign's 'class, not parity' gap.
why: Separates how much of ES's tail is explained by the sign layer (characters) vs the class layer; quantitative version of FRONTIER's F6/G4 split.
first_step: Quantify: fraction of variance of log s(p) explained by the quadratic-character vector of p modulo ℓ ≤ 100 (linear/tree model).

title: OEIS anchor: ordered count O(n) = A292581, at primes A292624
connection: O(n) (ordered triples) matches A292581, and O(p) matches A292624; U(p) matches A192789.
why: Three independent OEIS entries anchor the prime-restricted counts used in all correlation items below.
first_step: Pull b-files of A292624/A192789 to extend our prime data past 2·10⁵ for free, if they go further.

title: OEIS anchor: min max-denominator = A337432
connection: Our minz(n) (least possible largest denominator) matches A337432; it is the 'smallest-z' ES fingerprint.
why: A small minimal z is a constructive certificate; the entry may contain a conjectured growth bound useful as a heuristic target.
first_step: Read A337432 comments for a conjectured bound minz(n) ≪ n^{1+ε} or similar; compare to our records 2,3,10,14,33,52,102,138,232,…

title: U(p) at least-QNR-record primes is only moderately small
connection: At the least p≡1(4) with least QNR q (q=11..47), U(p)/log²p = 0.40,0.37,0.54,0.53,0.36,0.29,0.60,0.53,0.55,0.67,0.61 — below typical (≈1–2) but not record-hard; 2521 (least QNR 11) is far harder (0.15).
why: Shows hardness is not a function of the least QNR alone: p−1 smoothness / p ≡ 1 mod higher prime powers adds a second axis — useful for designing a two-parameter hardness model.
first_step: Regress log U(p) on log L(1,χ_p) and log(σ(p−1)/(p−1)) jointly; check which explains 2521 vs 87481.

title: n ∤ minlcm(n) ⟺ 4 | n
connection: The least common denominator of a solution of 4/n is divisible by n except exactly when 4 | n (data n ≤ 30 000; OEIS A008586 match for the exception positions).
why: Trivial direction: 4|n gives 4/n = 1/(n/4)·… with smaller lcm; but the converse (n | lcm for 4 ∤ n) is a clean lemma ensuring p-adic content of every solution.
first_step: Prove: if 4 ∤ n then every solution's lcm is divisible by n (consider v_q of both sides for q^a ∥ n).

title: minlcm(p)/p at primes not in OEIS; correlates +0.23 with least QNR
connection: The least common denominator over solutions, divided by p, behaves like a cost: larger when small primes are QRs (ρ=+0.23 with least QNR, +0.20 with L(1,χ_p)).
why: Smallest common denominator = smallest N with 4N/p a sum of three divisors of N (Egyptian-fraction 'practical number' view) — links ES to practical numbers / Erdős–Graham denominators.
first_step: Check: is minlcm(p)/p always a practical number? Compute and compare to OEIS A005153.

title: U(n) records at 2,3,6,8,10,12,15,24,30,40,48,60,… vs highly composite numbers
connection: Record positions of U(n) (not in OEIS) are dominated by smooth numbers but are not A002182 (15, 30, 40 appear; 36 does not).
why: Records of a divisor-sum-like count should track the extremal order of a specific divisor function; identifying it gives the right 'max U(n) ≍ ?' growth.
first_step: Compare record positions with records of Σ_{d|n} τ(d)², τ(n)τ(n+1)…; fit max_{n≤X} U(n) vs exp(c log X/log log X).

title: Easy primes: U(p) records eventually all ≡ −1 (mod 840)
why: Mirror of the hard primes (≡ 1 mod 840): ES-easiest primes are ≡ −1 modulo highly composite numbers (5039 = 7! − 1 = 2·2520 − 1). The count is a function of p's position relative to smooth numbers.
first_step: Note 55439 = 2·27720 − 1 and 5039 = 2·2520 − 1 are records; test the next candidates 2·lcm(1..k) − 1 and lcm(1..k) − 1 when prime; OEIS search of the record list gave no match.
alt_first_steps: [fingerprint-0037] Check if record primes satisfy p+1 = smooth with record τ(p+1); OEIS search of the record list (no match).

title: Campaign hard-prime lists are not in OEIS
why: No hidden classical identity (e.g. 'primes p with property X of p−1') explains them — or OEIS lacks it; submission would expose them to outside pattern-finders.
first_step: Submit the R-zero list with a definition and b-file to OEIS; also add I3 zeros (114 terms) and U failures.

title: R(3^k) = 0 exactly for even k (squares) and k = 1
why: Sanity fingerprint of T1 on prime powers; also the odd-power values (2,2,4,18,10,10) are a small test sequence for any closed formula.
first_step: Compare R(3^{2j+1}) with the BM main term M_BM(3^{2j+1}).

title: W(n) (all words) has records at 1,3,5,7,11,17,19,23,35,47,59,71,…
connection: Records of W(n) = #{t,u,v ≥ 1 : tuv−u−v = n} are at n with n+1 and 2n+1, 3n+1… all highly divisible (W counts divisors of tn+1 in classes); not in OEIS.
why: W(n) = Σ_t #{d | tn+1 : d ≡ −1 (mod t)} is the unrestricted analogue of the ES certificate count — its extremal behaviour bounds all sub-counts.
first_step: Identify W(n) with a classical divisor-sum (Σ_t τ_{−1 mod t}(tn+1)); submit to OEIS.

title: Uv zero set (all residues): 12, 28, 60, 96, 105, 124, 156, 204, 228, 288, …, 2961, …
connection: Without the n ≡ 1 (4) restriction, U-zeros are mostly even (multiples of 4 with n+1 prime-ish); non-OEIS.
why: Restricting the certificate condition to n ≡ 1 (4) loses nothing; the even zeros are an artefact — clarifies scope of U.
first_step: None beyond recording; possibly characterise the even zeros as n with n+v having no divisor ≡ −1 (mod v) for every allowed v.

title: ES counts at Sophie Germain / safe primes
connection: Safe primes (p = 2q+1) have p−1 maximally non-smooth; predicted to be ES-easy. Compute mean U(p)/log²p over safe primes vs all primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) (safe primes > 7 are ≡ 3 (mod 4)… so compare within class).
why: Tests the p−1 smoothness axis independent of p mod 4 (within p ≡ 3 (4), which is always ES-easy but count still varies).
first_step: Compute on p ≡ 3 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵: ρ(U, P⁺(p−1)) and mean over safe primes.

title: Number of distinct x vs number of solutions per x: concentration index
connection: U(p)/nx(p) (solutions per first denominator) is a concentration fingerprint; Gini coefficient of the x-profile per prime.
why: If solutions concentrate on few x, ES at p reduces to few divisor problems — relevant to POINTWISE strategies.
first_step: Compute U/nx at p ≤ 2·10⁵ (both in data) and its dependence on χ_p.

title: Linear-algebra fingerprint: rank of the solution set's denominator matrix mod small primes
connection: For each p, collect (x,y,z) mod q (q = 3, 5, 7) of all solutions; the occupied residue patterns form a fingerprint; compare across hard and easy primes.
why: Local solution patterns at q are exactly what covering congruences use; hard primes should occupy few patterns.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁴ (needs solution lists — extend the counter to dump solutions).

title: Composite n: is U(n) multiplicative-ish? (U(pq) vs U(p), U(q))
connection: Compute-and-check: for n = pq ≤ 30 000, regress log U(pq) on log U(p), log U(q).
why: ES for composites is inherited from prime factors; quantifying how the count lifts tells whether the 'solution sheaf' is multiplicative.
first_step: Use f4_all_30000.txt; scatter log U(pq) − log U(p) − log U(q).

title: Binary expansion of hard primes: no signal expected (null test)
connection: Hamming weight / trailing-ones of p in binary for the 40 hardest vs random p ≡ 1 (24): any difference beyond v₂(p−1) would be surprising.
why: Sanity test of the 'digits are irrelevant' prior; only v₂(p−1) (trailing zeros of p−1) is arithmetic.
first_step: Compute and record; expect null after conditioning on v₂(p−1).

title: Hard-prime 'deficit vectors' over local primes
connection: For each hard prime compute the vector ((q/p))_{q≤47} and 1[q | p+3], 1[q | p−1]; cluster hard primes by these vectors.
why: If hard primes form a few clusters (e.g. 'all small q QR' and 'p−1 smooth'), each cluster may need a different certificate family.
first_step: k-means on the 200 hardest primes ≤ 2·10⁵ with these binary features.

title: Isosceles solutions (two equal denominators) exist at a prime iff p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (or p = 2)
connection: The primes ≤ 10⁵ with no solution having x = y or y = z are exactly the 4 783 primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) (OEIS first-20 match: A002144 Pythagorean primes); composite failures ≤ 3000 start 25, 65, 85, … (all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4?).
why: A clean exact statement linking ES degenerate solutions to sums of two squares; the obstruction for p ≡ 1 (4) in the degenerate locus is exactly the hard class — a 'degenerate T1'.
first_step: Prove: 4/p = 2/x + 1/z or 1/x + 2/z solvable ⟺ p ≢ 1 (4) (reduce to a two-term problem 4/p − 2/x = 1/z, a divisor-in-class condition, show it needs a divisor ≡ 3 (mod 4) of something like p²); check composite failure set = n with all prime factors ≡ 1 (4) (A004613).

title: x | z ⟺ y | z for every solution at a prime (proved from the normal form)
connection: Since p | z, 4z/p = z/x + z/y + 1 is an integer identity: if x | z then z/y is an integer, and conversely. Data agree (identical failure sets and share 0.377).
why: Suggests a structural lemma: at a prime, x | z forces y | z (and conversely), i.e. z = lcm(x, y) — a rigid sub-family amenable to a parametrisation by divisors of z/p.
first_step: Use the lcm-closed family z = lcm(x, y) as a parametrisation by divisors of z/p (three divisors a, b of z with a + b + 1 = 4z/p).

title: Full chain x | y | z fails at 670 primes ≤ 10⁵, starting 73, 193, 313, 337, 409, 457, 577, …
connection: Chains exist for most primes but fail at a sizeable set containing the hard primes 193, 409, 577, 1201 (not in OEIS).
why: The chain sub-family is a 1-parameter-poorer certificate; its failure set is a hardness filter between the full ES and single lines.
first_step: Compute the density of chain failures among p ≡ 1 (24) vs others; is it ≈ constant (then infinitely many failures) or decaying?

title: Solutions with x prime fail at 4 597 primes; with some perfect-square denominator at 3 134
connection: Prime smallest denominators (share 0.7%) and square denominators (0.8%) are rare; failure sets start 31, 37, 53, 73, … and 17, 29, 41, 73, 89, … (no OEIS match).
why: Rare-shape sub-families give no ES leverage but are fingerprints for 'random-like' behaviour of denominators (density of primes/squares among x).
first_step: Compare the share of prime x with 1/log x heuristics (≈ 1/log(p/4)).

title: 'Only z divisible by n' fails at all powers of 2 (composites ≤ 3000)
connection: At n = 2^k every solution has ≥ 2 denominators divisible by n (or none); at odd primes the k₁-shape always exists.
why: Powers of 2 are the ES 'easy' case but structurally degenerate; sanity fingerprint for the normal-form lemma.
first_step: None.

title: Targeted search for record-hard primes via the fitted model
connection: Rank candidate primes p ≡ 1 (mod 840) up to 10¹² by predicted log U (Euler product over q ≤ 50 + 2-adic depth + τ((p+3)/4)) and compute U only for the top predictions.
why: Finds the hardest ES primes at scales where exhaustive counting is impossible — the best stress-test inputs for any proposed certificate family.
first_step: Implement: sieve p ≡ 1 (840) with all q ≤ 23 QR, then rank by τ((p+3)/4) and v₂(p−1); count U at the top 100 in [10⁹, 10¹⁰].

title: Hard primes vs Wilson / Wolstenholme-type congruences: null test
connection: Wilson quotients (p−1)!+1)/p mod p and Wolstenholme quotients are p-adic invariants of small integers collectively; test correlation with residual U(p).
why: Expected null (ES counts depend on quadratic data); a non-null would be surprising and important.
first_step: Compute Wilson quotient mod p for p ≤ 2·10⁵ (O(p) each — use p ≤ 2·10⁴) and Spearman.

title: U(n) at Sylvester-sequence-related n (2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, …)
connection: Sylvester numbers s_k satisfy 1 = Σ 1/s_i + 1/(s_k − 1); n = 43, 1807 = 13·139: compute U and compare to neighbours.
why: Numbers with built-in unit-fraction identities might have anomalously many ES solutions (an 'easy family' mirror of lcm+1).
first_step: Look up U(43), U(1807) in f4_all_30000.txt; extend to 3263443 = s₅ with the count program.

title: Ramanujan-sum expansion of the normalised ES count
connection: Compute-and-check: least-squares coefficients a_q in U(n)/log³n ≈ Σ_{q ≤ Q} a_q c_q(n) over n ≤ 30 000.
why: If a_q is (nearly) multiplicative with a_p ≈ −1/p-ish, the count has an Euler-product singular series over n — the all-n analogue of the χ_p law at primes.
first_step: Implement c_q(n) = Σ_{d | gcd(q,n)} μ(q/d) d and fit.

title: OEIS A392469 = records of min k (p | y = kp) over primes p ≡ 1 (mod 24) — reproduced
why: Identifies the entry's implicit restriction (p ≡ 1 mod 24) — a possible clarification for OEIS — and links its comment '(q/p) = 1 for q ≤ 13 for all late terms' to our χ_p Euler-product law.
first_step: Email/edit suggestion for A392469: state the p ≡ 1 (24) restriction or add the all-prime variant; compare k(p) with Cmin(p) of the (★) line.

title: A392469's empirical bound k(p) < 71 log p vs our certificate-size laws
connection: Gold notes k(a(n)) < 71·log a(n) for all known records; our (★) Cmin has mean ≈ 2 with rare large values (23105 at a boundary case), and Vmin ≤ 116 ≤ 3·10⁶.
why: Logarithmic certificate size is exactly what a 'small-certificate covering' approach needs; comparing the k(p) law with the line-specific laws tells which line has the best size profile.
first_step: Plot max_{p ≤ X} k(p)/log p from mink_pr_2e5.txt and compare with Vmin, Cmin records.

title: A257843 (Hasler): n where the lexicographically first solution ≠ the max-z solution
why: A 'solution-geometry' fingerprint (shape of the solution set's extremes) — a cheap invariant that may separate hard from easy classes.
first_step: Compute the density of A257843 among p ≡ 1 (24) vs others and correlate membership with residual U(p).

title: Lowest-count composites: are they products of hard primes?
connection: Rank composite n ≤ 30 000 by U(n)/log³n; test whether the lowest are products of two primes both in the hard class (p ≡ 1 mod 24) such as 73·193.
why: If hardness multiplies, composite ES-hardness reduces to prime hardness (expected: composites inherit solutions from each factor, so they should be easy).
first_step: Sort f4_all_30000.txt by U/log³n restricted to composites.

title: ES count vs number of prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) of n
connection: For composite n, fit log U(n) on ω₁(n) = #{p | n : p ≡ 1 (4)} and ω₃(n); the isosceles law says ω₃ = 0 kills degenerate solutions for odd n (even n have them anyway); does ω₃ also boost the bulk count?
why: Quantifies how the 'sum of two squares' structure of n influences ES counts beyond the isosceles locus.
first_step: Regress on f4_all_30000.txt.

title: Ratio y/x and z/y spectra as fingerprints of identity families
connection: Polynomial identity families produce solutions with rational ratios y/x → constants as p grows (e.g. y ≈ 2x); peaks in the empirical distribution of y/x identify which identities fire.
why: A data-driven way to rediscover Mordell-type identities and to see which ones the hard classes lack.
first_step: Histogram log(y/x) over all solutions at p ≤ 2·10⁵ split by class mod 840.

title: Hard-prime 'twin' structure: p and p + 2520 both hard?
connection: Because hardness depends on p mod 840 and quadratic characters, p and p + 840k share the mod-840 part but not the characters at q ∤ 840; test correlation of residuals at lag 840 among primes.
why: Separates the periodic (mod 840) from the character part: lag-840 correlation among primes estimates their variance shares (cf. 0.60 autocorrelation over all n).
first_step: Compute residual correlation for prime pairs (p, p+840k), k ≤ 10.

title: Fingerprint of 'ES at p' vs 'ES at 4p+1' / 'ES at (p+3)/4'
connection: The (★) divisor form involves 4Cp + 1 and the greedy step (p+3)/4; test whether U(4p+1) or U((p+3)/4) (when composite, often easy) correlates with U(p).
why: Cheap check of whether ES difficulty propagates along the natural 'p-tied integer' maps (a dynamical view: forests in FOREST_*.md).
first_step: Compute Spearman(U(p), U(4p+1)) for p ≤ 7 500 and Spearman(U(p), U((p+3)/4)).

title: Screening tool: certify-or-not table for any new certificate family
