connection: Generalise the variant counter to take a predicate plug-in and output failure sets at primes ≤ 10⁵ in < 1 min (as done for 32 shapes here).
why: Lets other lanes turn 'connection' items into falsifiable data within minutes — the variant runs here found single-exception families (lcm-closed: only 2521) that no theory predicted.
first_step: Refactor scripts/z52b_fingerprint_variants*.c into a predicate-driven engine with a small DSL (divisibility, coprimality, size).

title: Near-equal denominator perturbations
connection: Write y=z+h and study the exact residual equation as h varies, connecting ES to near-square factorization.
why: Small h gives structured, checkable subfamilies without claiming they cover every prime.
first_step: Enumerate the smallest attainable difference z−y for primes below 1000.

title: Cancellation across auxiliary parameters
connection: Sum character errors over C before taking absolute values, looking for cancellation lost in parameterwise bounds.
why: Different certificate lines may compensate each other's arithmetic biases.
first_step: Compute signed nonprincipal-character contributions for C≤30 over a sample of primes.

title: Local densities as fingerprints
connection: Compute exact residue-level densities for several certificate families and use the vector of densities as a fingerprint of p.
why: Local fingerprints might predict complementary families without asserting a local-global principle.
first_step: Enumerate admissible parameter tuples modulo 8,9,5,7 for three exact identities.

title: Uniform parameter thresholds
connection: Track how the smallest successful auxiliary cutoff grows separately in each arithmetic stratum.
why: A precise growth target can suggest which analytic estimate would actually be sufficient.
first_step: Compute running maxima of the least successful C and report them against log p and powers of p, with bounded-search caveats.

title: Proof-producing set cover
connection: Compress a finite verified range into exact identity templates plus a certified set-cover computation.
why: The output remains a finite-range proof, but it makes coverage mechanisms auditable.
first_step: Take 100 primes and export the chosen identities with exact substitution witnesses for each covered prime.

title: Sunflower patterns among constraints
connection: Search for families of certificate conditions sharing a common core and disjoint extra congruence requirements.
why: A sunflower structure may identify a reusable common lemma with several interchangeable completions.
first_step: Represent each small family by its set of atomic congruence conditions and detect common-core collections.

title: Finite-state rational transducers
connection: Search for digit-wise rules mapping p to candidate denominator digits with bounded carry memory.
why: A successful rule on a well-defined input language could become an explicit infinite family.
first_step: Synthesize a transducer for one already verified congruence family and inspect which extra states are needed to enlarge its domain.

title: Integer programming with witness cuts
connection: Use integer programming on a linearized auxiliary formulation, adding exact cuts learned from failed modular assignments.
why: A solver can discover useful constraints while all final witnesses remain directly checkable.
first_step: Linearize one bounded factor-allocation model and add only cuts proved from its congruence equations.

title: Annealing with exact repairs
connection: Combine stochastic descent on a congruence energy with deterministic repair of one remaining divisibility condition.
why: A repair step ties the physical analogy to exact arithmetic output.
first_step: Implement a toy annealer on one residual parametrization and verify every reported zero by integer arithmetic.

title: Parallel tempering across families
connection: Allow searches at different energy scales or in different parametrization charts to exchange states through exact chart maps.
why: Exchanges may overcome family-specific traps if the maps are valid and reversible on their domains.
first_step: For two charts with a known overlap, test state exchanges on bounded rational points before imposing integrality.

title: Syntax-guided parametrizations
connection: Define a grammar of gcd, floor, product, and reciprocal operations and search short candidate certificate programs.
why: A restricted grammar makes discovery auditable and encourages explicit formulas rather than opaque predictions.
first_step: Enumerate expressions of depth at most three and test exact identities on a training set before symbolic checking.

title: Abstract interpretation of parameters
connection: Propagate intervals, congruence classes, and sign information through a candidate denominator program.
why: A sound abstract domain can prove that many inputs produce positive integers without enumerating them.
first_step: Implement transfer rules for addition, multiplication, and exact division on interval-congruence pairs.

title: Modular conflict learning
connection: When a parameter box fails for a provable modular reason, store that reason as a reusable nogood.
why: Learned conflicts can apply across many primes sharing the same local labels.
first_step: Extract one sound modular conflict clause from a failed bounded search and test its reuse on other instances.

title: Proof-carrying witness search
connection: Make each search result carry the integer arithmetic needed to verify positivity and the cleared identity independently.
why: This decouples experimental algorithms from trust in their implementation.
first_step: Specify a compact witness record and a verifier using only exact integer operations.

title: Independent arithmetic verification
connection: Check generated triples by two algebraically distinct routes: cleared products and reduced rational sums.
why: Independent formulations can catch implementation errors or malformed records.
first_step: Write a small verifier specification and test it against deliberately corrupted triples.

title: Minimum-description-length family selection
connection: Balance the coverage of a formula against the complexity of its exceptional-case conditions.
why: This discourages overfitting while keeping every mathematically valid family available.
first_step: Encode formula syntax and residue exceptions with an explicit code, then compare several portfolios on held-out primes.

title: Levin-style program search
connection: Dovetail candidate certificate programs with budgets depending on program length.
why: This gives a systematic discovery baseline and highlights the cost of the chosen expression language.
first_step: Enumerate a tiny arithmetic-program language and allocate execution steps by a prefix-code weight.

title: Fair interleaving of infinite families
connection: Run countably many valid parameter searches in a schedule that eventually explores every finite parameter tuple.
why: Fairness prevents one expensive family from starving other methods, without guaranteeing ES itself.
first_step: Specify a diagonal schedule over family index and parameter height and prove every finite tuple is reached.

title: Dominance pruning of partial certificates
connection: Define a sound partial-order dominance relation between search states with identical arithmetic obligations.
why: A dominated state can be removed only when every completion has a no-more-expensive counterpart.
first_step: Prove one dominance rule based on equal residue state and remaining factor inventory, then measure pruning.

title: Modular fingerprints for duplicate detection
connection: Use several modular reductions to cheaply reject unequal symbolic or numerical certificates before exact comparison.
why: Fingerprints accelerate deduplication while exact fallback prevents collisions from becoming false identities.
first_step: Design a hash-plus-exact-check pipeline for canonical denominator triples and rational identity expressions.

title: Straight-line certificates for huge denominators
connection: Store denominators by exact arithmetic programs when their decimal expansions are unwieldy.
why: Compact descriptions can make recurrent or compositional families practical, provided equality is still verified exactly.
first_step: Encode a small recurrence family as straight-line programs and compare evaluation and verification costs.

title: Modular interpolation of identities
connection: Recover candidate polynomial coefficients from evaluations modulo several primes and reconstruct rational coefficients.
why: This can make symbolic discovery cheaper, followed by exact identity checking.
first_step: Recover a known low-degree numerator identity from modular samples as a pipeline sanity check.

title: Batch gcd across parameter values
connection: Compute shared factors among many p-tied auxiliary integers using gcd relations and batch techniques.
why: Shared factors can be extracted without factoring every value separately.
first_step: For fixed p and bounded C, derive pairwise gcd restrictions and compare batch extraction with individual trial division.

title: Factor-base relations for certificate search
connection: Collect auxiliary values smooth over a chosen factor base and record their residue-selection structure.
why: This borrows a relation-collection viewpoint without assuming factorization-style linear algebra directly solves ES.
first_step: Build a tiny factor-base relation matrix and determine what additional condition turns a relation into an actual target divisor.

title: Factoring-free gcd certificates
connection: Search for constructions where a useful divisor is produced as a gcd of two explicit expressions.
why: A gcd can supply a verified factor without requiring complete factorization.
first_step: Try short polynomial gcd expressions in p and C and retain only cases where the gcd provably has the target residue.

title: Certified prime selection for experiments
connection: Separate primality verification of test inputs from ES witness verification so arithmetic strata remain trustworthy.
why: Misclassified inputs could distort experiments about prime-only behavior.
first_step: Specify a test-data format carrying primality evidence or a reproducible deterministic primality procedure alongside each p.

title: Memory-bounded parallel parameter search
connection: Split the auxiliary domain into deterministic chunks with no shared giant divisor table.
why: A streaming design enables much broader evidence collection without uncontrolled Cartesian-product allocations.
first_step: Specify chunk sizes, per-worker memory caps, and an exact merge key for a bounded search prototype.

title: Cache keys as mathematical assumptions
connection: Key cached computations by the full parametrization, modulus, positivity convention, and search bounds.
why: This prevents results from one mathematical model being silently reused in a different one.
first_step: Audit a toy search cache and construct two deliberately incompatible configurations that must not share entries.

title: Decision trees as conjecture extractors
connection: Fit shallow trees using residue and character features, then translate each leaf into a proposed arithmetic lemma.
why: A transparent leaf condition is a concrete object for proof or counterexample search.
first_step: Fit a depth-three tree for one family's success and exhaustively test each leaf condition in a larger range.

title: Counterfactual feature interventions
connection: Alter one arithmetic feature in synthetic parameter data while holding the exact algebraic model fixed where possible.
why: This helps distinguish genuine mechanisms from correlated labels in observational prime data.
first_step: Within one residue-compatible family, vary a single auxiliary prime factor and measure the resulting target-residue change.

title: Uncertainty-guided experiment allocation
connection: Allocate computation to prime strata where count models disagree rather than only to predicted hardest cases.
why: Disagreement can expose model misspecification and broaden the exploratory dataset.
first_step: Compare two simple count models and search a balanced sample of their largest disagreement cases.

title: Matched prime pairs
connection: Pair primes with nearly identical cheap arithmetic features but very different least witness costs.
why: Contrasts can isolate information missing from a proposed selector.
first_step: Match on residues modulo a small modulus and several character labels, then inspect auxiliary factorizations of the largest-cost contrasts.

title: Semantic retrieval of equivalent equations
connection: Search literature by algebraic shape and alternate terminology rather than only by the phrase Erdős–Straus.
why: Relevant results may use norm equations, reciprocal partitions, or restricted divisor sums under different names.
first_step: Form five precise search queries from the equation (ay−b)(az−b)=b² and inspect the returned definitions.

title: Replayable symbolic proof traces
connection: Export each algebraic simplification as a sequence of exact transformations rather than only a final yes/no answer.
why: A small checker can replay discovery-tool output independently.
first_step: For one rational identity, record clearing denominators, ring normalization, and hypothesis use as separate trace steps.

title: Metamorphic tests from scaling
connection: Use exact transformations such as scaling a valid triple along with n to generate consistency checks.
why: If 4/n=Σ1/x, scaling all four quantities by a positive integer preserves the identity.
first_step: Specify a test transforming a valid witness at n into one at kn and verify all fields update consistently.

title: Beyond polynomial parametrizations
connection: Explore rational, recurrent, floor-based, and piecewise arithmetic witness formulas as genuinely different representation classes.
why: A limitation of one formula class need not rule out another, and each class has explicit verification obligations.
first_step: Write one toy certificate rule in each representation class and list exactly how its identity and domain would be proved.

title: Finite covers that expose square conditions
connection: Pass to a cover adjoining the square root of a discriminant and examine whether the lifted equation becomes simpler.
why: The cover records an exact arithmetic condition rather than assuming every base point lifts.
first_step: Construct the discriminant double cover of a quadratic slice and write its rational-point map back to certificates.

title: Inverse descriptions of bounded failure
connection: Ask what common structure is forced when many explicitly chosen certificate mechanisms all fail for one input.
why: An inverse statement could turn a failure pattern into the hypothesis of a different constructive family.
first_step: For three exact families, combine their failure congruences and derive the simplest remaining arithmetic condition without treating it as a global obstruction.

title: Backward construction from a desired last step
connection: Start with the final exact integrality or positivity lemma a certificate proof would need, then solve backward for parameter choices satisfying it.
why: Backward search can produce identities that forward enumeration misses, with every reverse step checked algebraically.
first_step: Choose a target congruence for a complementary divisor, substitute it into the residual equation, and solve for one remaining auxiliary parameter.

title: Coupling-from-the-past / exact sampling of ES solutions to detect non-uniformity
connection: Propp–Wilson exact sampling of a uniformly random solution of 4/p; the sampling chain's mixing time as a function of p is a measurable complexity of the solution set.
why: If exact sampling is easy (chain couples fast), solution sets are 'structured'; structure is what a proof can exploit.
first_step: Design a Markov chain on solutions (moves: change one of (c,d,f) parameters in the Type I form) and measure coupling time for p ≤ 10⁵.

title: Program synthesis (enumerative/DreamCoder) for a 'solution formula' with branching on residues
connection: Search the space of programs 'if p ≡ r mod M then (x,y,z) = (polynomials in p)' with sqrt/floor allowed (non-polynomial! escaping Mordell–Schinzel) that output a valid ES solution on as many primes as possible.
why: Mordell–Schinzel kills polynomial identities on square classes; identities with floor, gcd, or ⌊√p⌋ are not covered by that theorem and nobody has systematically searched them.
first_step: Define a DSL: polynomials in p, ⌊√p⌋, ⌊p/k⌋, gcd(p+a, b), residue branching; run enumerative search (depth ≤ 6) scoring on primes ≡ 1 mod 840 up to 10⁵; report best coverage.
refs: Mordell–Schinzel (no polynomial identity on square classes)

title: Reverse-engineer Salez's 10¹⁷ verification code for implicit structure (which identity family covers which prime)
connection: Salez's verification used a specific set of identities/searches; the *distribution of which family fired first* across primes up to 10¹⁷ is data nobody has analysed for structure.
why: A 'which rule saved this prime' census is a cheap large-scale pattern-discovery dataset.
first_step: Locate Salez's paper/code (arXiv 1406.6307 'The Erdős–Straus conjecture: new modular equations and checking up to N=10^17'); re-run the family census for p ≤ 10⁹ and tabulate first-firing family vs p mod 840.

title: Boolean function analysis: Fourier spectrum of the indicator 'C wins for p' as a function of p mod 4C·something
connection: For fixed C, whether 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C depends on p via the factorisation of 4Cp+1; its Fourier spectrum over p mod M (M a multiple of 4C) measures 'junta-ness'.
why: A low-degree Fourier concentration for all C would be a covering-ish structure; spectrum spread across high frequencies says the event is genuinely 'global'.
first_step: Compute, for C ≤ 20 and M = lcm(4C, 840), the Fourier spectrum (over ℤ/M) of E_p[win_C(p) | p ≡ r mod M] for p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Automated theorem proving on the 'two-term' lemma with a free parameter: Vampire/E on the divisor form
connection: First-order provers can sometimes prove number-theoretic lemmas given axioms about divisibility; the lemma 'if p ≡ 1 mod 24 and p < 2^k then ∃C ≤ K ...' is a bounded statement they might handle for small k.
why: Low chance, but the prover's search traces for small k might reveal which lemmas are reused — a proof-skeleton extraction.
first_step: Encode the divisor form in TPTP with Peano arithmetic axioms + bounded quantifiers; try Vampire for k ≤ 8.

title: Monte-Carlo tree search over 'proof strategies' for small residue classes (AlphaZero for covering systems)
connection: The search for a covering system of identities is itself a game tree; MCTS/RL has found covering-type constructions in other settings (e.g. Wagner's RL for combinatorial counterexamples). Target: maximal density of primes ≡ 1 mod 840 coverable by degree-≤2 identities with moduli ≤ M.
why: Not a proof, but establishes the best achievable 'partial cover' and whether the uncovered set has structure (squares + ?).
first_step: Reproduce the known cover (Mordell + Salez families) as a baseline; implement the RL search over identity templates; report uncovered density vs M.
refs: Wagner, 'Constructions in combinatorics via neural networks' (2021)

title: Model-checking a finite abstraction: ES for p 'with all small primes' residues fixed' as a finite transition system
connection: Abstract p by its residues mod all primes ≤ B and by its Legendre symbols; a finite-state system over these abstractions can be model-checked for the property 'some C ≤ K yields a divisor in class'. Counterexample traces are candidate hard residue profiles.
why: Finds the exact abstract profile of a potential counterexample; such profiles could then be hunted at 10¹⁸ (adversarial search guidance).
first_step: Enumerate profiles of p mod 840 and Legendre symbols (q/p) for q ≤ 31; for each profile, compute the empirical fraction of primes with C_min ≤ 10; find worst profiles.

title: Database cross-reference: OEIS sequences around f(n), C_min, and Egyptian-fraction lengths
connection: OEIS has A073101 (number of solutions of 4/n), A192787, etc. Looking at the 'sequences that reference these' and their formulas/comments may reveal a connection the campaign missed.
why: Cheap and occasionally very fruitful.
first_step: Fetch OEIS A073101, A192787, A192788, A192789 and all sequences citing 'Erdős–Straus'; read comments and formulas; list any with unexpected cross-references (e.g. to class numbers, Bernoulli, Markoff).

title: Bit-level pattern mining on winning C in binary (are winning C's 'smooth'? 'prime'? 'powers of 2'?)
connection: The multiplicative structure of winning C matters (4C is the modulus); test whether winning C are biased toward smooth numbers, primes, or specific residue classes mod 3, 5, 7.
why: A bias (e.g. winning C is often a multiple of 3 for p ≡ 1 mod 3) is a candidate identity direction; cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ collect all winning C ≤ 1000; compare their distribution of ω(C), smoothness, C mod 12 against the uniform baseline.

title: De Bruijn / universal cycle: does a single 'universal' residue sequence of C's cover all primes up to X with O(log X) entries?
connection: Hitting-set problem: find the smallest set S of C's such that every prime p ≤ X has a winner in S. Its growth |S(X)| in X (constant? log X? X^ε?) is the 'covering dimension' of ES.
why: If |S(X)| = O(log X) with a nice structure (e.g. S = {1,2,3,6,...} products of small primes), a 'nested cover' proof shape emerges.
first_step: Greedy set-cover on the prime–C incidence matrix for p ≤ 10⁷, C ≤ 10⁴; report |S| vs X.

title: Gaps between consecutive winning C at fixed p: bounded? polylog?
connection: For fixed p, the set of winning C is infinite (e.g. once one C wins, multiples? no — not obviously closed under multiplication; check). The gap structure of winning C's is a 1-D sequence per p whose 'syndeticity' would be a strong structural fact.
why: If winning C's for each p are syndetic with uniformly bounded gaps (say gap ≤ G for all p ≥ p₀), then 'some C ≤ G wins' — a bounded cover, which Mordell–Schinzel suggests is false for polynomial covers but maybe true as a non-polynomial fact. The data decides.
first_step: Compute winning C ≤ 10⁵ for 100 primes near 10⁶; measure max gap; check closure properties (is C winning ⟹ kC winning for some k's?).

title: Design theory: do winning (C, a)-pairs form a block design over residue classes of p mod M?
connection: A covering design covers all k-subsets by blocks; here, blocks = {p mod M : (C, a) wins} for each (C, a); ES = covering of all prime residues. The 'covering number' structure of the block system might have a design-theoretic description (e.g. it's a union of cosets of subgroups of (ℤ/M)^×).
why: Design-theoretic regularity (each residue covered equally often) is exactly the kind of structure a uniform argument needs; irregularity points at hard residues.
first_step: For M = 840, compute for each residue r the number of (C, a) pairs with C ≤ 50 that win for ALL primes ≡ r (i.e. polynomial identities) and for a positive fraction; display as a matrix.

title: Experimental: histogram of (c, d) parameter pairs of ALL Type I solutions across primes — is the (c,d) 'mass' concentrated on few d?
connection: If most Type I solutions have d ∈ {1,2,3,5,…} small, then Type I is essentially a handful of imaginary quadratic fields; the per-d problem (class group of ℚ(√−d) fixed) is more rigid.
why: Reduces 'infinitely many (c,d)' to 'finitely many d with c varying' for the bulk of certificates — a dimension reduction for proofs.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, tabulate the fraction of primes whose FIRST Type I solution has d ≤ 10, and the fraction with ANY d ≤ 10 solution.

title: Experimental: 'd = 1 ∪ d = 2 ∪ d = 3' — do three fixed imaginary quadratic fields already certify all primes ≤ 10⁸ (Type I)?
connection: If yes, ES on that range follows from three class-group-structured problems; the question 'is there a p with no Type I solution for d ≤ 3' becomes the sharpened target with full algebraic structure (ℤ[i], ℤ[√−2], ℤ[ω]).
why: Fixed-field problems admit Chebotarev/ray-class analysis; a fixed finite set of fields with 'all p' coverage would be a new, cleaner conjecture.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁷ whether a Type I certificate with d ∈ {1,2,3} exists (c unbounded up to p); list failures and their count growth.

title: Experimental: 'second-smallest certificate' statistics — gaps between the first and second winning parameters
connection: If the second certificate typically appears soon after the first (small ratio), solutions cluster; if far, they are 'isolated events'. Clustering suggests a local structure around certificates (a 'neighbourhood rule' generating one from another).
why: Cheap, and a neighbourhood rule would be a dynamical structure.
first_step: Compute (C₂/C₁) for the two smallest winning parameters for p ≤ 10⁶; histogram.

title: Experimental mathematics: the 'Ramanujan-style' approach — find exact identities among ES counts and classical arithmetic functions by brute-force linear algebra (Wilf–Zeilberger-free)
connection: Compute vectors (f_I(n), f_II(n), f(n), τ(n), σ(n), r₂(n), r₄(n), h(−4n), H(4n−1)…) for n ≤ 2000 and search for integer linear/bilinear relations via LLL on the data matrix. Any exact relation (even conjectural) is structural gold.
why: Standard experimental-math technique; cheap; a positive hit would redirect the campaign.
first_step: Build the matrix, run PSLQ/LLL for relations with small coefficients among ≤ 10 functions; validate hits on n ≤ 10⁵.

title: Experimental: generating-function fitting — is Σ f_II(n) q^n a quasi-modular form up to a small error?
connection: Test numerically whether the q-series of ES counts (or sub-counts) is close to a combination of Eisenstein series E₂, E₄ and theta functions: compute the coefficients, fit by least squares to a basis of modular forms of small weight/level, check residuals.
why: If a sub-count is quasi-modular, its coefficients have asymptotic formulas with explicit error (Deligne/Rankin–Selberg), potentially pointwise; a quick fit is the test.
first_step: Compute f_II(n) for n ≤ 5000; fit to the space spanned by divisor-sum functions σ_k(n), σ_k(n/2), r_k(n); report residual norm.

title: Reverse direction: from the exceptional-prime data, construct 'ES-hard' pseudo-random primes by CRT to stress-test at 10²⁰ (profile engineering)
connection: Take the Legendre profiles of the C-form exceptions and of the adversarial primes; construct primes ≈ 10²⁰ with the same profile mod all primes ≤ 50 (CRT + primality search); measure f(p). If the profile predicts hardness, we've found a 'hardness invariant'; if not, hardness is not profile-driven.
why: Direct test of the Legendre-profile hypothesis, which underlies several items here.
first_step: Compute profiles of 409, 577, 5569, 9601 and the repo's hardest primes; CRT-construct 100 primes near 10¹⁵ per profile; compute Type I/II counts on small parameters.

title: Tool: use Pari/GP's `factor` with `factorint` flags (ECM) to push the C-form census to p ≤ 10⁷ and C ≤ 10⁴ cheaply; publish the exceptional list to OEIS
connection: The C-form exceptional primes (409, 577, 5569, 9601, …) form a natural integer sequence not (apparently) in OEIS; computing it to 10⁷ and submitting it creates a public hook for others.
why: Community/visibility item with a concrete deliverable; OEIS entries attract exactly the kind of elementary-number-theory attention that could explain the exceptions.
first_step: Run the census (Pari, ~hours); check OEIS for the sequence; draft an OEIS submission with the definition 'primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) with no C ≤ 10⁴ such that 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C'.

title: The subset-product failure set S_C has a 'dimension' δ_C = 1 − (fraction of residue classes that can contribute): compute δ_C for all C ≤ 100 and its asymptotics
connection: For S_C defined by 'subset products of prime factors (mod 4C) avoid −1', a first-order density exponent is obtained by the largest −1-free subgroup H ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× (density of primes in H = |H|/φ(4C)); 'all factors in H' has counting function x/(log x)^{1 − |H|/φ(4C)}. The maximal −1-free subgroup has index 2 (any subgroup not containing −1 can be enlarged to index 2? Not always: in (ℤ/8)^× = {1,3,5,7}, −1 = 7; −1-free subgroups: {1}, {1,3}, {1,5} — index 2 exist ✓. In general, −1 ∉ H means H ∩ ⟨−1⟩ trivial; H can be extended to a complement of ⟨−1⟩ if the group is... (ℤ/4C)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × stuff; −1 may or may not be a 'direct summand' — e.g. in ℤ/4 (cyclic), −1 = 2 is the unique element of order 2, every nontrivial subgroup contains it! So for (ℤ/4C)^× containing a cyclic ℤ/4 summand in which −1 lies... concretely for 4C = 20: (ℤ/20)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/4 with −1 = ? ; the −1-free subgroups may have index 4.) So δ_C varies non-trivially with C — compute it.
why: δ_C controls how 'hard' it is for a prime to fail at C: small δ_C (large −1-free subgroup) = easy to fail; the C with largest δ_C are the most 'useful' certificates; a proof would use them. Possibly δ_C → 1 along C with (ℤ/4C)^× having −1 'deeply embedded' (e.g. 4C = 4q with q ≡ 1 mod 4 prime? then (ℤ/4q)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/(q−1), −1 = (1, (q−1)/2); −1-free subgroups can have index 2: take {0} × ℤ/(q−1)? contains (0,(q−1)/2) ≠ −1 = (1, (q−1)/2) ✓ index 2. Hmm so index 2 always possible? Need −1 ∉ some index-2 subgroup ⟺ −1 is not a square… ⟺ some character χ mod 4C with χ(−1) = −1 (odd character) — ALWAYS exists for 4C ≥ 3. So index-2 −1-free subgroups always exist: δ_C ≤ 1/2 for all C.) So every C has δ_C = 1/2 at the top level — failure at C costs exactly (log)^{-1/2}·(const_C). Then the heuristic failure density for all C ≤ K is (log p)^{−K/2}·Π const_C, where const_C encodes the finer structure. Verify.
first_step: For C ≤ 100: list all −1-free subgroups, their indices; confirm index 2 always achievable; compute the full generating-function density of S_C (sum over all failure patterns, not just 'all in H') numerically for 4Cp+1 ≤ 10⁷.

title: For p = 409, tabulate the factorisation type of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 1000: how does 'no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C' happen each time (prime? all factors ≡ 1 mod 4C? subgroup?)
connection: Direct forensic analysis of the exception: a histogram of failure reasons for one prime across C.
why: If the failures are 'random-looking' (mixture of reasons), 409 is a statistical accident and larger C must win (contradicting the C ≤ 60000 search — making an obstruction likely); if a single reason dominates (e.g. all factors always in a particular subgroup), the obstruction is visible.
first_step: Compute and classify; compare with a control prime (401 or 433) where the C-form wins quickly.

title: ES for n = t² + 1 and n = 4t² + 1: compute identities and check whether the campaign already knows 'ES holds for all n = t² + 1'
connection: n = t² + 1: 4/(t²+1) — try x = (t²+1)/… hmm t² + 1 ≡ 1,2 mod 4; for t even n ≡ 1 mod 4. Is there a known identity? e.g. 4/(t²+1) = 1/(t²+1)·4; want 1/A + 1/B + 1/C. Note (t² + 1) + t² ... Possibly known in the literature on 'Erdős–Straus for n = polynomial values' (e.g. 'all n of the form k² + 1'?). Search.
why: If identities exist for square-avoiding polynomial families, that's an infinite family of hard-class n (not primes necessarily) — and the proof technique (polynomial in t) shows how T1 is dodged; worth 30 minutes.
first_step: git grep -il 't^2+1\|t² + 1\|k^2+1' -- '*.md'; brute-force search for identities with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[t] of degree ≤ 4 for n = t² + 1, 4t² + 1, t² + t + 1.

title: Sturmian words / Beatty sequences: the set of x with ⌊4x/p⌋ jumps, and the 'three-gap theorem' as a structure on candidate denominators
connection: The first denominator x in 4/p = 1/x + … must satisfy p/4 < x ≤ 3p/4 (for 3 terms); the candidate set and the remainders (4x − p)/(px) are governed by the Beatty-like sequence ⌊4x/p⌋; the three-gap theorem (Steinhaus) describes gap structures of such sequences — possibly organising the 'which x leaves a two-term remainder' question.
why: Structural organisation of the x-search; cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, mark the x in (p/4, 3p/4] whose remainder is a two-term Egyptian fraction; study the gap distribution between marked x vs three-gap predictions.

title: Crowd computing: a BOINC/Folding-style project to extend ES verification to 10²⁰ AND collect the certificate census (which form fires first) as a public dataset
connection: Verification alone is of limited value, but a *structured* census (per prime: smallest C-form, smallest Type I d, smallest e-slice) at scale creates a dataset for pattern discovery and for testing the exceptional-set rate predictions.
why: Public datasets attract analysts; the compute is embarrassingly parallel.
first_step: Write the census kernel (fast C: trial division of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10³) and estimate throughput; publish the 10¹²-range dataset first.

title: Compression of proofs: measure the description length of the 'certificate table' for all primes ≤ X as a function of X — the best possible 'proof length' of ES restricted to [1, X]
connection: If ES has no uniform proof, the shortest certificate table for primes ≤ X should grow like π(X)·(bits per certificate) with no compression; if a hidden uniform rule exists, compression beats this. Kolmogorov-style; measurable with real compressors on the sorted (p, C_min, a) table.
why: A direct, if crude, test for hidden uniformity, complementary to ML items.
first_step: Produce the table to 10⁷, compress with xz and with a specialised model (arithmetic coder conditioned on p mod 840); compare bits/prime to the entropy of C_min's empirical distribution.

title: Exceptional primes vs the 'u = 1, 2, 3 classical identities': 409 + 1 = 410 = 2·5·41 (all odd factors ≡ 1 mod 4), 411 = 3·137 (3 ≡ 3 mod 8, 137 ≡ 1), 412 = 4·103 … — build the 'residue avoidance table' for p + u, u ≤ 50, for 409 and for a random control
connection: A table showing, for each u, the prime factors of p + u mod 4u and why no subset product is ≡ −1 — the 'forensics' item in the additive form, where it is readable by hand.
why: Hand-readable evidence is the fastest route to a conjecture about the obstruction type.
first_step: Generate the table; look for the pattern (e.g., 'every odd prime factor q of p + u satisfies (q/409) = +1 or q ≡ 1 mod 4u' — a Legendre-symbol coincidence pattern).

title: ES with distinct denominators vs. allowing repeats — trivial reductions sanity table
connection: ES allows x=y; distinct version is equivalent for large n? ↔ known small cases.
why: Cheap sanity: if distinct ES fails at some p while ES holds, that's a data point about solution-set rigidity.
first_step: Compute primes ≤ 10⁷ where all solutions have a repeated denominator (expect none beyond tiny p).

title: Extreme value theory for max over p ≤ X of (minimal certificate size)
connection: Gumbel/Fréchet laws for maxima of iid ↔ max_p min-certificate as function of X.
why: If the max grows like (log X)^a with EVT-consistent fluctuations, extrapolate beyond 10¹⁸; deviations flag structure.
first_step: From repo census data, extract record-setting primes for 'least u in I3 word' and fit EVT growth.

title: Records sequence of hardest primes as an OEIS-style object
connection: Sequence of primes p where min certificate size exceeds all previous ↔ OEIS has such records for ES? (check).
why: Records concentrate structure (adversarial primes); their pattern (residues, factorisations of p±small) suggests failure mechanisms.
first_step: Search OEIS for 'Erdos-Straus' sequences; compute records for 'smallest x in 4/p = 1/x+…' and submit/compare.

title: Maximum entropy model for certificate distribution given residue constraints
connection: MaxEnt with constraints p mod q for q ≤ Q ↔ best prediction of R(p) from local data.
why: The gap between MaxEnt prediction and actual R(p) is the 'global' part; if it's small, ES difficulty is local-plus-noise.
first_step: Fit log R(p) ~ Σ_q β_q·1[p ≡ a mod q] by regularised regression and report R² vs Q.

title: Boltzmann sampling of certificates for very large p (10^100)
connection: Analytic combinatorics Boltzmann samplers ↔ draw random (u,C) weighted by 1/(4uC−1) and test divisibility.
why: Monte Carlo estimates of R(p) at astronomical p (where full enumeration is impossible) test whether the main term persists; finds adversarial p faster.
first_step: Implement weighted sampling over (u,C) for p ~ 10^50 random primes ≡ 1 mod 840 and estimate hits per 10⁹ samples vs M(p) prediction.

title: Model checking / BDDs for residue-class coverage up to large modulus
connection: Binary decision diagrams represent huge residue-class sets compactly ↔ the uncovered set after modular filters.
why: Exact representation of the uncovered set mod M (M huge) enables precise density of residual primes and structure detection.
first_step: Represent uncovered residues mod 840·Π small primes as a BDD over CRT digits; measure size growth.

title: ILP / MIP solvers on the ES Diophantine equation with bounds
connection: Integer programming with nonlinear constraints ↔ certificate search; branch-and-bound gives infeasibility certificates for bounded boxes.
why: Infeasibility certificates (dual bounds) for 'no certificate in box' are mechanical proofs of local non-existence; could expose structure in hard primes.
first_step: Formulate 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) with x ≤ y ≤ z bounds in a MINLP solver (SCIP) for p=409 restricted to Type II (★) and inspect the infeasibility proof.

title: Distributed computing / BOINC-style verification to 10^19 or 10^20
connection: Verification frontier 10^18 ↔ volunteer computing (like PrimeGrid) could extend it; also gives data on hardest primes.
why: Not proof progress, but extends EVIDENCE and adversarial data; community engagement.
first_step: Estimate cost: Mihnea–Dumitru's runtime per 10^18 and the extension cost; check PrimeGrid/yoyo@home interest in number-theory side projects.

title: Meta: canonical certificate database for p ≤ 10⁹ (minimal certificate per form)
connection: Downloadable data ↔ ML items and statistical items in this list need it.
why: Shared data accelerates all experimental items.
first_step: Generate and store compressed minimal (u,C) per prime ≤ 10⁹ (Type II (★)) and minimal Type I; document format.

title: Near-miss gap g(p) = min{4/p − (1/x+1/y+1/z) > 0} and its distribution
connection: Egyptian under-approximations ↔ ES ⟺ gap 0 attainable; the minimal positive gap measures how 'close' p is to failure in a continuous sense.
why: If hard primes have systematically larger minimal positive gaps, gap-based potential functions might guide search or reveal a continuous invariant.
first_step: Compute g(p)·p³ (or appropriately normalised) for primes ≤ 10⁵ restricted to small denominators; compare hard vs easy primes.

title: First-term offset k: x = (p + 4k + 3)/4 and the binary remainder (4k+3)/(px)
connection: Choosing x = ⌈p/4⌉ + k leaves (4k+3)/(p·x) to be written as 2 unit fractions (Rav criterion: divisors d₁,d₂ of p·x with (4k+3) | d₁ + d₂) ↔ a 1-parameter family of binary problems.
why: Gives a simple 'search depth' measure k*(p); a bound k*(p) ≤ (log p)^A would be an ES-strength conjecture with a clean shape for probabilistic modelling (each k succeeds with probability ~ τ(px)/(4k+3)).
first_step: Compute k*(p) for primes ≤ 10⁸ and its max growth; model success probability per k via divisor counts of px.

title: Transport between nearby primes: 4/p = 4/q + 4(q−p)/(pq)
connection: If q close to p has a solution and the correction 4(q−p)/(pq) combines nicely ↔ continuity-type arguments (rare in arithmetic).
why: Likely dead (corrections need extra terms), but checking whether 'ES(q) + small structure ⟹ ES(p)' for q − p ∈ {4, 8, 12} ever works is cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, test whether some solution of 4/q (q = p+4k prime) shares two denominators with a solution of 4/p; record frequency.

title: Correlations R(p) vs R(p + 840k): local vs global difficulty
connection: Primes in the same class mod 840 share local data ↔ if R/M is strongly correlated for p, p + 840k, difficulty is local; if not, global randomness.
why: Quantifies the 'lottery' model; complements the ML feature-importance item.
first_step: Compute correlation of R(p)/M_BM(p) and R(p')/M_BM(p') for prime pairs with p' − p = 840k, k ≤ 100.

title: Pocklington/Proth-style primality certificates as anti-certificates: when 4Cp+1 is prime, slice C fails
connection: Proth: N = k·2^n + 1 primality tests ↔ 4Cp+1 = (4C)·p + 1 is Pocklington-friendly (p | N − 1).
why: Every C with 4Cp+1 prime kills slice C; such C are certifiable cheaply. A counterexample prime p needs many such C or other failure modes; the density of 'Pocklington-prime C' for hard p is a measurable stress quantity.
first_step: Count C ≤ 10⁴ with 4Cp+1 prime for (★)-failing primes vs random primes; compare with Hardy–Littlewood prediction.
